SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-b contributes the adaptive design framework: prospective, concurrent/ad hoc, and retrospective adaptations, plus the concern that unplanned adaptations can drift the enrolled population from the target population and inflate type I error.
Paper-c contributes conjoint-analysis evidence from 108 AD study partners: home visits had the highest utility (0.89) and offset high-risk disutility (-0.85); car service was redundant; 17% would participate with amenities alone, 27% with home visits, 60% with low risk/high active-treatment chance; burden correlated with AD severity.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use paper-c’s quantified participation utilities as a pre-specified adaptation trigger inside paper-b’s prospective adaptive design. Enrollment/retention could be monitored; if they fall below threshold, the trial prospectively adds home visits—not as an ad hoc amendment—to preserve the originally targeted AD population and control type I error. Paper-c supplies the causal content of the adaptation; paper-b supplies the regulatory/statistical frame.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
A two-stage AD trial-design study. Stage 1: administer the paper-c conjoint survey to study partners at screening. Pre-specify an adaptive rule: at interim, if cumulative enrollment <70% of target or dropout >15%, offer home visits to all subsequently enrolled participants. Measure enrollment, dropout, partner burden (ADL, NPI), and baseline utilities. Validate by comparing actual acceptance of home-visit offers with conjoint-predicted acceptance. Stage 2: simulate an AD trial using observed utilities and retention patterns under fixed vs. adaptive home-visit conditions; compute sample representativeness and empirical type I error under a null treatment effect. Proposed hypothesis: the pre-specified home-visit adaptation improves retention and reduces target-population drift compared with fixed design while maintaining type I error. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no available source directly tests adaptive AD trial designs, so the transferability of paper-c’s utilities to adaptive-trial decisions is proposed, not established.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose an adaptive AD trial where home visits are triggered by pre-specified enrollment/retention thresholds. Conjoint-derived utilities from paper-c define the intervention; paper-b’s prospective adaptive framework defines its timing and validity. A pilot-plus-simulation design tests whether this reduces population drift, improves retention, and controls type I error beyond either paper alone.

FINAL IDEA: A prospectively adaptive AD trial using conjoint-derived home-visit utilities as a pre-specified enrollment trigger should reduce participation-related population drift while controlling type I error.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b supplies the distinction between prospective, concurrent/ad hoc, and retrospective adaptations, and the concern that unplanned changes can shift the enrolled AD sample from the target population and inflate type I error.  
Paper-c supplies conjoint utilities from 108 AD study partners: home visits had utility 0.89, offsetting high-risk disutility −0.85; car service was redundant; participation rose to 27% with amenities and 60% with low-risk/higher active-treatment chance; burden correlated with AD severity.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
I adopt Researcher B’s use of conjoint utilities as pre-specified enrollment/retention thresholds inside a prospective adaptive design, and qualify Researcher C’s “retention weights” by requiring the adaptive rule to be fixed before enrollment, not selected post hoc. Home visits become the only triggered amenity because paper-c shows car service adds little, avoiding redundant adaptations.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Stage 1: administer a conjoint survey to 200 AD study partners, replicating paper-c’s four attributes and adding one adaptive attribute: mid-trial switch to home visits. Estimate utilities and interaction with AD severity.  
Stage 2: simulate an AD trial where enrollment/retention are functions of those utilities. The prospective adaptive rule is: if cumulative enrollment <70% or dropout >15% at interim, offer home visits to all subsequent participants. Compare three designs: fixed, adaptive using only statistical stopping rules, and preference-triggered adaptive. Validate Stage 1 by testing whether predicted home-visit preference replicates paper-c’s 0.89 utility; validate Stage 2 by benchmarking predicted participation against paper-c’s 27% amenity gain and by sensitivity analysis across null treatment scenarios to measure empirical type I error.  
Missing cross-paper knowledge: neither paper tested mid-trial preference change, so Stage 1 is required.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We propose an AD trial design in which a single pre-specified amenity—home visits—is triggered by enrollment/retention thresholds, using paper-c’s conjoint utilities to define the trigger and paper-b’s prospective framework to preserve validity. Simulation and conjoint replication test whether this reduces population drift and controls type I error.

FINAL IDEA: A prospectively adaptive AD trial using conjoint-derived home-visit utilities as a fixed enrollment/retention trigger should reduce participation-related population drift while controlling type I error.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b contributes prospective vs. ad hoc/retrospective adaptations and warns that unplanned changes can drift the enrolled AD sample from the target population and inflate type I error. Paper-c contributes conjoint utilities from 108 AD study partners: home visits (0.89) offset high-risk disutility (−0.85); car service is redundant; participation rises from 17% with amenities alone to 27% with home visits and 60% with low-risk/higher active-treatment chance.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
I adopt paper-b’s prospective adaptation as the validity constraint, and qualify paper-c’s fixed-attribute utilities as not directly transferable to mid-trial adaptation without new conjoint data. I reject car-service adaptation as paper-c shows no added utility over home visits. The operational link: pre-specify a rule before trial start—if cumulative enrollment <70% of target or predicted 6-month retention <80% at interim, trigger home visits, requiring the conjoint-predicted home-visit utility ≥0.89 and using alpha-spending to preserve type I error. Home-visit utility acts through reduced travel/partner burden to improve retention, thereby reducing paper-b’s population drift.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Stage 1: conjoint survey of 200 AD study partners replicating paper-c’s four attributes plus mid-trial home-visit switch; estimate utilities. Validate by reproducing paper-c’s benchmarks: home-visit utility ≈0.89, participation shift 17%→27% with home visits, 60% with low-risk/high-treatment. Stage 2: simulate AD trials where enrollment/retention probabilities are functions of Stage 1 utilities. Compare fixed, standard prospective adaptive, and preference-triggered home-visit adaptive designs. Measure type I error under null, retention, time to full enrollment, dropout, and population drift on ADL/NPI distributions. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source directly measures mid-trial preference effects, so Stage 1 tests transferability.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We propose a pre-specified adaptive AD trial in which home visits are triggered by enrollment/retention thresholds using conjoint-derived utility from paper-c within paper-b’s prospective framework. Conjoint replication and trial simulation test whether this reduces preferential dropout and population drift while controlling type I error.

FINAL IDEA: A pre-specified adaptive AD trial that triggers home visits using paper-c’s conjoint utility as a threshold within paper-b’s prospective framework should reduce population drift and preserve type I error.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b reviews adaptive clinical trial designs, distinguishing prospective, concurrent (ad hoc), and retrospective adaptations, and warns that unplanned modifications may alter the patient population and inflate type I error.  
Paper-c provides conjoint-analysis utilities from 108 Alzheimer’s disease study partners, showing home visits (utility 0.89) can offset high intervention risk disutility (-0.85), while car service adds little; predicted participation rises from 17% to 27% with amenities and to 60% with higher active-treatment chance.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Conjoint-derived utilities become quantitative enrollment/retention weights inside a prospective adaptive design. Preference data do not merely describe willingness; they operationally drive pre-specified adaptation rules—e.g., add home visits if enrollment falls below a threshold—while keeping the adaptation prospective to control type I error.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Stage 1: administer a conjoint survey to 200 AD study partners, adding adaptive-design attributes (interim analysis frequency, sample-size re-estimation) to paper-c’s risk, home visit, transport, and active-treatment attributes. Estimate utilities.  
Stage 2: build trial simulations where enrollment/retention are functions of those utilities. Compare fixed, standard adaptive, and preference-weighted adaptive designs. Measure type I error under null scenarios, power, time to full enrollment, and retention. Validate by benchmarking predicted participation against paper-c’s 27% amenity increase and against a pilot AD trial recruitment dataset.  
Missing cross-paper knowledge: neither paper measures preferences for adaptive features nor links preference utilities to statistical operating characteristics; new conjoint and simulation data are required.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We propose preference-weighted adaptive designs that use AD study partners’ conjoint utilities for trial attributes to pre-specify adaptation rules, aiming to improve recruitment and retention without inflating type I error. Simulations and a pilot validation will test whether preference-informed adaptations outperform standard adaptive and fixed designs.

FINAL IDEA: Integrating conjoint-derived participant preferences into prospective adaptive trial rules can jointly optimize recruitment, retention, and statistical validity.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b distinguishes prospective, concurrent/ad hoc, and retrospective adaptations, warning that unplanned changes can shift the enrolled population and inflate type I error.  
Paper-c supplies conjoint utilities from 108 AD study partners: home visits (0.89) offset high-risk disutility (−0.85); car service adds little; participation rises from 17% with amenities to 27% with home visits and 60% with lower risk/higher active-treatment chance.  
I adopt paper-c’s utility estimates as baseline willingness weights. I reject treating them as direct causal effects of mid-trial adaptation without replication. I qualify paper-b’s validity concern as primarily relevant to non-prospective adaptations.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Use paper-c’s utilities to construct a pre-specified preference-weighted adaptation rule within paper-b’s prospective framework. At interim, if observed enrollment is below target or predicted dropout exceeds a threshold, the trial adds home visits only when the predicted utility gain (e.g., 0.89 vs baseline) exceeds a pre-specified cost/utility threshold. Because the trigger and change are pre-specified, it remains prospective rather than ad hoc, preserving type I error control.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Stage 1: administer a conjoint survey to 200 AD study partners, replicating paper-c’s attributes plus trial-stage attributes: interim monitoring frequency, mid-trial switch to home visits, transport, risk. Estimate utilities; validate by checking expected home-visit utility ≈0.89 and the predicted participation shift reproduces paper-c’s 17%→27%/60% benchmarks.  
Stage 2: simulate AD trials comparing fixed, standard prospective adaptive, and preference-weighted adaptive designs. The preference-weighted rule selects home-visit adaption at interim using Stage 1 utilities plus pre-specified alpha-spending. Measure type I error, power, time to full enrollment, dropout, and population drift (baseline ADL/NPI distributions vs target). Validate simulation inputs with Stage 1 utilities; no source directly measures mid-trial adaptation effects, so Stage 1 directly tests transferability.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We propose a preference-weighted prospective adaptive AD trial in which conjoint-derived utilities define home-visit adaptation triggers. A two-stage conjoint validation plus simulation will test whether this reduces enrollment-related population drift and dropout while controlling type I error.

FINAL IDEA: Preference-weighted prospective adaptive AD trials using conjoint-derived home-visit utility as a pre-specified adaptation trigger can reduce population drift while preserving statistical validity.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b distinguishes prospective, concurrent/ad hoc, and retrospective adaptations, warning that unplanned changes can shift the enrolled population and inflate type I error. Paper-c provides conjoint utilities from 108 AD study partners: home visits utility 0.89 offset high-risk disutility −0.85; car service was redundant; participation rose from 17% with amenities to 27% with home visits and 60% with low-risk/high-active-treatment chance; burden correlated with AD severity.  
Adopt paper-b’s prospective pre-specification as the validity constraint. Adopt paper-c’s home-visit utility as the adaptation content. Qualify paper-c’s fixed-attribute utilities: they cannot be assumed to transfer to mid-trial changes without new measurement. Reject car-service adaptation because paper-c shows redundancy.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Use paper-c’s conjoint utilities to define a pre-specified home-visit trigger inside paper-b’s prospective adaptive design. At interim, if cumulative enrollment <70% or dropout >15%, offer home visits only when predicted utility gain from a new conjoint model exceeds a pre-specified threshold (e.g., utility ≥0.5). Because trigger and change are fixed before trial start, the adaptation remains prospective rather than ad hoc, preserving type I error control.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Stage 1: conjoint survey of 200 AD study partners replicating paper-c’s attributes plus a mid-trial home-visit switch and visit-frequency change; estimate utilities and interactions with AD severity. Validate by reproducing paper-c’s home-visit utility ≈0.89 and predicted participation near 27% with amenity.  
Stage 2: simulate AD trials with enrollment/retention as functions of Stage 1 utilities under fixed, standard prospective adaptive, and preference-triggered adaptive designs. Pre-specify alpha-spending; measure empirical type I error under null, power, time to full enrollment, dropout, and population drift using baseline ADL/NPI distributions. Missing cross-paper knowledge: direct effect of mid-trial adaptation on willingness is untested; Stage 1 tests transferability.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We embed AD study partners’ conjoint utilities for home visits into a pre-specified prospective adaptive rule. A two-stage conjoint validation and simulation test whether preference-triggered home visits reduce dropout and population drift without inflating type I error.

FINAL IDEA: A pre-specified home-visit adaptation triggered by paper-c-derived conjoint utilities within paper-b’s prospective adaptive framework reduces AD trial population drift while controlling type I error.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b reviews adaptive trial designs, distinguishing prospective, concurrent, and retrospective adaptations, and warns that post-adaptation changes can shift the enrolled population from the target population and inflate type I error. Paper-c provides conjoint-analysis utilities from 108 AD study partners: home visits had highest utility (0.89), offsetting high-risk disutility (−0.85); car service added little; utility varied with patient severity.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
I propose that preference utilities from paper-c can serve as retention weights in paper-b’s prospective adaptation rule. If an adaptation changes visit burden, transport, or risk, its predicted effect on study-partner willingness can be used to select adaptations that reduce non-random dropout and keep the accrued sample closer to the target population.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
First, extend paper-c’s conjoint experiment to include adaptive attributes, such as mid-trial switch to home visits, added transport, or changed visit frequency, and estimate utilities in a new AD study-partner sample. Second, build a prospective adaptive trial simulation using paper-b’s framework. At interim analyses, candidate adaptations are selected by a composite score: statistical promise plus predicted preference utility, constrained by target-population representativeness. Compare preference-blind adaptation, preference-weighted adaptation, and no adaptation. Measure type I error, population drift, retention, and duration; validate with bootstrap and sensitivity analysis. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no available source directly tests whether mid-trial adaptations change willingness or whether preference-weighting reduces drift; this is a proposed hypothesis.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
Adaptive trials can drift from the target population when mid-trial changes alter burden or risk. This project embeds study-partner preference utilities, estimated by conjoint analysis, into prospective adaptation rules for AD trials. Simulation will test whether preference-weighted adaptations improve retention and representativeness without inflating type I error.

FINAL IDEA: Adaptive clinical trial designs should incorporate conjoint-estimated participant/study-partner preferences as retention weights in adaptation rules to reduce population drift and preserve validity.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b contributes the prospective adaptive design framework and warns that unplanned adaptations can drift the enrolled population from the target and inflate type I error. Paper-c contributes conjoint utilities from 108 AD study partners: home visits had utility 0.89 and offset high-risk disutility (−0.85); car service was redundant; predicted participation increased from 17% with amenities alone to 27% with home visits and 60% with low risk/higher active-treatment chance.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Adopt paper-b’s prospective adaptation frame and paper-c’s home-visit utility as a quantitative retention trigger. Qualify paper-c’s estimates: they were measured for fixed trial attributes and cannot be directly transferred to mid-trial adaptations, so new conjoint data are needed. Reject car-service adaptation because paper-c reports it adds little beyond home visits. The mechanism is a pre-specified rule: if interim enrollment or retention falls below a target, add home visits only when the predicted utility from the conjoint model exceeds a threshold, keeping the change prospective to control population drift.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Stage 1: extended conjoint survey with 200 AD study partners, adding adaptive attributes—mid-trial home-visit switch, visit-frequency change, risk, and active-treatment chance. Stage 2: simulate an AD trial where enrollment and retention probabilities are functions of estimated utilities; compare fixed, standard adaptive, and preference-weighted adaptive designs. Measure type I error under null, retention, time to full enrollment, and population drift. Validate by reproducing paper-c’s benchmarks: amenities-only participation near 17–27% and low-risk/high-treatment near 60%. Missing cross-paper knowledge remains whether preference-triggered adaptations improve representativeness without inflating type I error.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
This project embeds conjoint-derived home-visit utilities into prospective adaptive rules for AD trials. A new conjoint survey and trial simulation test whether preference-weighted adaptations reduce dropout and population drift while controlling type I error.

FINAL IDEA: Pre-specified adaptive rules using conjoint-derived home-visit utilities can reduce AD trial population drift and preserve type I error.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b contributes the adaptive-design taxonomy—prospective, concurrent/ad hoc, retrospective—and warns that adaptations can shift the enrolled sample from the target population and inflate type I error. Paper-c contributes conjoint utilities from 108 AD study partners: home visits had utility 0.89, offsetting high-risk disutility −0.85; car service was redundant; participation rose from 17% with amenities to 27% with home visits and 60% with low-risk/higher active-treatment chance.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Adopt Researcher B’s prospective pre-specified trigger and home-visit-only choice; reject car-service adaptations because paper-c shows they add little. Qualify paper-c utilities as fixed-design willingness estimates, not yet causal effects of mid-trial change. The mechanism: before enrollment, specify that at interim if enrollment <70% or predicted dropout >15%, the trial adds home visits to all subsequent participants only when the conjoint-predicted home-visit utility meets a pre-specified threshold (e.g., ≥0.80). This keeps the amenity prospective rather than ad hoc.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Stage 1: administer a conjoint survey to 200 AD study partners, replicating paper-c’s four attributes plus one adaptive attribute—mid-trial switch to home visits. Validate by testing whether home-visit utility is equivalent to 0.89 (margin ±0.15) and whether predicted participation reproduces paper-c’s 17%/27%/60% pattern. Stage 2: simulate an AD trial where enrollment and retention are functions of Stage 1 utilities. Compare fixed, standard prospective adaptive, and preference-triggered adaptive designs. Measure type I error under null, time to full enrollment, retention, and population drift using baseline ADL/NPI distribution differences. Validate simulation by benchmarking participation probabilities to paper-c. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source measures adaptation-induced preference change, so Stage 1 directly tests transferability.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We propose a preference-triggered prospective adaptive AD trial in which home visits are added at interim only if conjoint-predicted utility exceeds a pre-specified threshold. A two-stage conjoint validation plus simulation tests whether this reduces dropout and population drift while controlling type I error.

FINAL IDEA: A prospective adaptive AD trial using conjoint-derived home-visit utility as a fixed interim trigger can reduce participation-related population drift while preserving statistical validity.

nodes.text:
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper B reviews adaptive clinical trial designs and warns that mid-trial adaptations can shift the enrolled patient population, threatening type I error control and the original scientific question.  
Paper C uses conjoint analysis in Alzheimer’s disease study partners, showing home visits had the highest utility and could offset high intervention-risk disutility; reducing travel burden was associated with willingness to participate, especially by patient severity.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Adaptive design changes are also participation-relevant design changes. The proposed mechanism is to use conjoint-estimated utilities as quantitative inputs to adaptive trial simulations: candidate adaptations—such as adding home visits, car service, or altering randomization probabilities—change expected participation and retention across patient subgroups. This preference-weighted enrollment model is embedded in adaptive decision rules that select modifications maintaining the target population composition while improving recruitment. Thus Paper B’s adaptation framework controls statistical risk, while Paper C’s utilities predict who actually enrolls or remains under each adaptation.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
1. Build a preference-weighted enrollment/retention model from Paper C’s utilities and severity correlates (ADL, NPI).  
2. Simulate an adaptive AD trial comparing standard adaptations versus preference-constrained adaptations. Outcomes: type I error, power, population drift, time to full enrollment, retention.  
3. Validate with a new conjoint survey of AD study partners that includes stated participation choices under candidate adaptations; compare predicted versus stated enrollment decisions.  
Missing cross-paper knowledge: Paper C measures stated preferences, not actual trial enrollment; Paper B provides no preference data. Calibration of utilities to real participation rates must be established.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
This project integrates adaptive trial methodology with patient-preference research by using conjoint utilities from Alzheimer’s study partners to constrain adaptive design choices. Simulations will test whether preference-weighted adaptations reduce population drift and preserve type I error while improving recruitment and retention. Validation uses a new conjoint survey linking preferences to participation choices. The contribution is a statistically safer, participation-informed adaptive trial design framework.

FINAL IDEA: Use Alzheimer’s study partners’ conjoint utilities to constrain adaptive trial design decisions, testing whether preference-weighted adaptations reduce population drift and preserve validity while improving recruitment and retention.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper B classifies adaptive designs as prospective, concurrent/retrospective, warns adaptations may shift patient population and inflate type I error, and requires pre-specification.  
Paper C provides conjoint utilities from 108 AD study partners: home visits utility 0.89 offset high-risk disutility -0.85; car service redundant; willingness correlated with AD severity and burden.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
I adopt Researcher C’s pre-specified trigger, not Researcher B’s treatment of “adaptation type” as a conjoint attribute, since Paper C never measured adaptation type utility. I qualify Paper C’s utilities as stated preferences, not observed enrollment. The mechanism: embed home-visit utility as an interim adaptation rule in a prospective adaptive AD trial. At n=50, if retention <70% and baseline home-visit utility ≥0.89, switch subsequent participants to home-visit follow-up. This uses Paper C’s strongest preference result to constrain Paper B’s adaptation decision while preserving the original target population definition.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Simulation: compare fixed vs preference-triggered adaptive design on type I error, power, population drift, recruitment time, retention. Use ADAS-Cog as primary outcome; measure caregiver burden, AD severity, travel burden, and re-administer conjoint utilities.  
Pilot validation: run a two-stage AD trial with the above pre-specified trigger; after adaptation, compare predicted vs actual enrollment/retention using new conjoint responses. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no existing data link adaptive logistics changes to AD clinical outcomes or actual retention; calibration of utilities to real participation rates must be established.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
Adaptive designs risk validity, while AD trials struggle with participation. This project uses Paper C’s home-visit utility as a pre-specified trigger in Paper B’s prospective adaptive framework. Simulation and pilot test whether preference-driven logistical adaptation improves retention without inflating type I error or shifting the enrolled population, extending both statistical and preference-based trial design.

FINAL IDEA: Use AD study partners’ conjoint-derived home-visit utility as a pre-specified interim adaptation trigger to improve retention while controlling type I error and population drift.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper B classifies adaptive designs as prospective, concurrent, or retrospective and warns that unplanned adaptations can shift the enrolled population and inflate type I error unless pre-specified.  
Paper C provides conjoint utilities from 108 AD study partners: home-visit utility 0.89 offset high-risk disutility -0.85; car service was redundant; reduced travel burden correlated with AD severity.

ADOPT/REJECT/QUALIFY  
Adopt the pre-specified home-visit utility as an interim trigger. Adopt Paper C’s home-visit utility but qualify it as a stated preference requiring calibration to actual enrollment. Reject treating “adaptation type” as a patient-facing conjoint attribute and reject car service as redundant.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Use Paper C’s home-visit utility as a prospective, pre-specified adaptation rule inside Paper B’s adaptive framework. At n=50, if retention <70% and the calibrated predicted retention gain from adding home visits exceeds a utility-derived threshold (≥0.89), switch subsequent participants to home-visit follow-up. The threshold is chosen by simulation under the null to hold type I error ≤5% and limit population drift.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Pilot two-arm AD trial (n=120), primary ADAS-Cog. Stage 1 measures baseline conjoint utilities, AD severity, caregiver burden, and actual retention under clinic visits. Fit a logistic calibration from stated utility to observed participation. Use this in simulation to set the interim threshold. At interim apply trigger; Stage 2 follows home-visit or clinic arm. Compare type I error, power, recruitment time, retention, and covariate drift against a fixed design. Validate by re-administering conjoint post-interim and comparing predicted versus actual Stage 2 participation. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no existing data jointly link adaptive logistics changes to AD outcomes; this study generates them.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
Adaptive designs risk population drift, while AD trials struggle with retention. This project embeds AD study partners’ conjoint-derived home-visit utilities into a prospective adaptive design as a pre-specified interim trigger, with calibration linking stated utilities to actual enrollment. Simulation and pilot test whether preference-triggered home visits improve retention without inflating type I error or shifting population composition.

FINAL IDEA: Use AD study partners’ conjoint-derived home-visit utility as a pre-specified, simulation-calibrated adaptive trigger to improve retention while controlling type I error and population drift.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-b contributes a taxonomy of adaptive clinical trial designs—prospective, concurrent (ad hoc), retrospective—and warns that adaptations may shift the actual patient population and inflate type I error; it also identifies implementation barriers and rare-disease strategies.
Paper-c contributes a conjoint-analysis method showing Alzheimer’s disease study partners value home visits (utility 0.89), which offsets high intervention risk disutility (-0.85); car service is redundant; inconvenience reduction correlates with disease severity and may increase participation.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use paper-c’s preference-measurement method to quantify willingness to participate under adaptation features described by paper-b. Operationally, “adaptation type” becomes a trial-design attribute in a conjoint experiment: fixed, prospective adaptive, or ad hoc amendment. Paper-b supplies the risk/validity features of these adaptations; paper-c supplies the mechanism linking design attributes and amenities to enrollment utility. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no existing data jointly measure adaptive-design features and participant preferences.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Recruit AD study partners and present hypothetical trial scenarios varying five attributes: adaptation type (fixed vs prospective vs ad hoc), home visits (yes/no), car service (yes/no), chance of receiving active intervention, and disclosed risk of altered trial validity/type I error. Measure willingness to allow participation. Hypotheses: prospective adaptation will have smaller disutility than ad hoc amendment; home visits will offset adaptation-related disutility. Estimate mixed logit utilities and predicted enrollment shares. Validate by comparing predicted participation with actual recruitment in a subsequent pilot AD trial using the highest-utility design.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This project tests whether prospective adaptive trial features can be redesigned to maintain AD study partner willingness by combining adaptive-design risk taxonomy with conjoint preference measurement. It quantifies how adaptation type, home visits, and intervention chance jointly predict enrollment. If home visits offset adaptation disutility, trialists could use preference-based redesign to reduce recruitment delays while monitoring adaptation-related validity risks.

FINAL IDEA: Integrating adaptive-design risk features from clinical trial methodology with conjoint preference measurement can predict and offset enrollment losses caused by trial adaptations in Alzheimer’s disease studies.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b contributes adaptive trial categories and warns that ad hoc adaptations can shift the enrolled population and inflate type I error unless pre-specified.  
Paper-c contributes conjoint-measured utilities: home visits had highest utility (0.89), offsetting high-risk disutility (-0.85); car service was redundant; reduced travel burden correlated with AD severity.

ADOPT/REJECT/QUALIFY  
Adopt Researcher C’s threshold-trigger idea, but qualify it as a prospective, pre-specified adaptation—not ad hoc—to preserve paper-b’s type I error constraint. Adopt Researcher A’s preference-weighted enrollment model for simulation, but reject treating stated utilities as actual enrollment probabilities without calibration. Reject car service as redundant from paper-c.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Use paper-c’s measured home-visit utility as a pre-specified interim trigger inside paper-b’s prospective adaptive design. At n=50, if observed retention <70% and mean baseline home-visit utility ≥0.89, the trial switches future participants to home-visit follow-up. This causally connects preference measurement to an adaptive decision rule: the trigger is fixed before data, not chosen ad hoc, thereby avoiding population drift.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Two-stage AD pilot plus simulation. Stage 1 enrolls AD study partners, measuring baseline conjoint utilities, AD severity, caregiver burden, and retention. Trigger as above. Compare type I error, power, recruitment time, and retention against a fixed design. Validate by re-estimating conjoint utilities at interim and comparing predicted participation under the triggered adaptation with actual enrollment in Stage 2. Also simulate a preference-weighted enrollment model that links paper-c utilities to observed retention rates via a calibration factor, testing whether the trigger reduces population drift. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source jointly measures adaptive logistics and AD outcomes; this study generates those data.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
Adaptive trials risk population drift, while AD trials struggle with retention. This project embeds conjoint-derived home-visit utilities into a prospective adaptive design as a pre-specified interim trigger. Simulations and a two-stage pilot test whether preference-driven logistical adaptation improves retention without inflating type I error, extending both preference measurement and adaptive methodology.

FINAL IDEA: Use AD study partners’ conjoint-derived home-visit utilities as a pre-specified trigger in prospective adaptive trials to improve retention while controlling type I error and population drift.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b contributes adaptive design taxonomy and warns that ad hoc adaptations can shift the enrolled population and inflate type I error unless rules are pre-specified.  
Paper-c contributes conjoint utilities from 108 AD study partners: home visits have highest utility (0.89), offsetting high-risk disutility (-0.85); car service is redundant; travel burden correlates with AD severity.

ADOPT/REJECT/QUALIFY  
Adopt Researcher C’s use of home-visit utility as a pre-specified trigger, but qualify that the utility threshold must be converted to a predicted retention gain through calibration, not used as a raw 0.89 cutoff. Adopt Researcher A’s preference-weighted enrollment model for simulation. Reject treating “adaptation type” as a patient-facing conjoint attribute; reject car service as redundant. Qualify paper-c’s utilities as stated preferences requiring calibration to actual retention.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Embed paper-c’s home-visit utility into paper-b’s prospective adaptive design as a quantitative interim rule. At a pre-planned interim, estimate predicted retention gain from adding home visits using a calibration model linking stated utility to observed retention. If observed retention <70% and predicted gain exceeds a simulation-calibrated threshold that controls type I error and population drift, switch future participants to home-visit follow-up. This connects preference measurement to an operational adaptation decision through a pre-specified, statistically bounded rule.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Two-stage pilot AD trial (n=120, ADAS-Cog primary outcome). Arm A: fixed home visits. Arm B: adaptive, adding home visits at interim if retention <70% and calibrated predicted gain exceeds threshold. Pre-specify threshold via null simulations. Measure retention, recruitment time, type I error, power, and baseline covariate drift. At interim, re-administer conjoint survey; compare predicted versus actual post-trigger retention to validate calibration. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no existing data link adaptive logistics changes to actual AD retention or clinical outcomes.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
Adaptive trials risk validity, while AD trials struggle with retention. This project embeds conjoint-derived home-visit utility into a prospective adaptive design as a simulation-calibrated trigger. A pilot tests whether preference-driven home visits improve retention without inflating type I error or shifting population composition, extending both preference measurement and adaptive methodology.

FINAL IDEA: Use AD study partners’ conjoint-derived home-visit utility as a simulation-calibrated threshold in a prospective adaptive trial to improve retention while controlling type I error and population drift.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper B reviews adaptive clinical trial designs, classifying them as prospective, concurrent, or retrospective, and warns that unplanned adaptations may shift the patient population and inflate type I error unless pre-specified.  
Paper C uses conjoint analysis in 108 AD study partners: home visits had the highest utility (0.89), offsetting high-risk disutility (-0.85); car service was redundant; low-risk/high-active-treatment predicted 60% willingness; reduced travel hassle correlated with AD severity.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Use Paper C’s measured utility weights as pre-specified adaptation thresholds inside Paper B’s prospective adaptive design. At interim, if enrollment/retention falls below a boundary or caregiver burden exceeds a utility-weighted threshold, the trial adds home visits for future participants. This connects preference measurement operationally to adaptive trial rules, not merely shared topic.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Simulation plus pilot two-stage AD trial. Primary outcome: ADAS-Cog change; measure caregiver burden, AD severity, travel burden, and baseline conjoint utilities. Pre-specify adaptation: at n=50, if observed retention <70% and home-visit utility ≥0.89, switch subsequent participants to home-visit follow-up. Compare type I error, power, recruitment time, and retention against a fixed design. Validate by re-estimating conjoint utilities in the enrolled sample and comparing predicted vs actual willingness. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source has joint data on adaptive logistics and AD outcomes; this study would generate it.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
Adaptive trials risk population drift, while AD trials struggle with recruitment and retention. This project embeds conjoint-derived participant preferences into a prospective adaptive design, using home-visit utility as a pre-specified interim trigger. Simulations and a pilot test whether preference-driven logistical adaptation improves retention without inflating type I error, extending both preference measurement and adaptive methodology.

FINAL IDEA: Use AD study partners’ conjoint-derived utilities for home visits as pre-specified adaptation triggers in prospective adaptive clinical trials to improve recruitment/retention while controlling type I error.

Revision note: I adopt Researcher A’s use of conjoint utilities as inputs to adaptive trial simulations, but reject Researcher B’s “adaptation type” as a conjoint attribute because prospective/ad hoc categories are not patient-facing. I qualify both: Paper C’s utilities are stated preferences, requiring calibration to actual enrollment.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper B reviews prospective, concurrent, and retrospective adaptive designs, warning that unplanned adaptations can shift the enrolled population and inflate type I error unless rules are pre-specified.  
Paper C provides conjoint utilities from 108 AD study partners: home-visit utility 0.89 offsets high-risk disutility -0.85; car service is redundant; reduced travel burden correlates with AD severity and increases willingness to participate.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Use Paper C’s home-visit utility as a pre-specified quantitative adaptation trigger within Paper B’s prospective adaptive design. At a planned interim, if retention falls below a boundary and the predicted retention gain from adding home visits exceeds a threshold derived from the utility (≥0.89), the remainder of the trial switches to home-visit follow-up. This threshold is chosen through simulation to hold type I error and population drift within pre-specified bounds, connecting preference measurement to adaptive decision rules.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Pilot two-arm AD trial (n=120) with ADAS-Cog as primary outcome. Arm A fixed home visits; Arm B adaptive, adding home visits at interim if retention <70% and home-visit utility threshold is met. Pre-specify boundaries via simulation under the null to control type I error. Measure retention, time to full enrollment, baseline covariate drift, and caregiver burden. Validate by re-administering conjoint survey post-interim and comparing predicted versus actual participation decisions; estimate calibration factor linking stated utilities to real retention.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
This project embeds AD study partners’ conjoint-derived home-visit utility into a prospective adaptive trial as a pre-specified trigger, chosen by simulation to preserve type I error and population composition. A pilot tests whether preference-triggered home visits improve retention without inflating error, extending both preference measurement and adaptive methodology.

FINAL IDEA: Use AD study partners’ conjoint-derived home-visit utility as a pre-specified adaptation threshold in a prospective adaptive trial to improve retention while controlling type I error and population drift.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper B classifies adaptive designs and warns unplanned adaptations can shift the enrolled population and inflate type I error unless pre-specified.  
Paper C provides conjoint utilities from 108 AD study partners: home visits highest utility (0.89), offsetting high-risk disutility (-0.85); car service redundant; travel-hassle reduction correlated with AD severity.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Revision: adopt a pre-specified threshold trigger; reject treating “adaptation type” as a patient-facing conjoint attribute; qualify Paper C’s utilities as stated preferences requiring calibration. Use Paper C’s home-visit utility as a pre-specified interim adaptation rule inside Paper B’s prospective adaptive design. At interim, if observed retention <70% and mean baseline home-visit utility ≥0.89, switch subsequent participants to home-visit follow-up. This connects preference measurement to an adaptive decision rule without ad hoc changes, preserving the original target population.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Simulation under null and alternative compare fixed vs preference-triggered design on type I error, power, population drift, recruitment time, retention. Pilot two-stage AD trial: measure baseline conjoint utilities, caregiver burden, AD severity, retention. Pre-specify the above trigger. After adaptation, re-administer conjoint survey; compare predicted participation from utilities with actual retention in Stage 2 and estimate a calibration factor mapping stated utility to observed behavior. Validate whether the trigger reduces drift while maintaining type I error. Missing cross-paper knowledge: joint data linking adaptive logistics changes to AD retention and outcomes.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
This project embeds AD study partners’ home-visit utility into prospective adaptive designs as a pre-specified interim trigger. Simulation and pilot test whether preference-driven logistical adaptation improves retention without inflating type I error or shifting the enrolled population, producing a calibrated preference-adaptive framework.

FINAL IDEA: Use pre-specified conjoint-derived home-visit utility thresholds as interim adaptation triggers in prospective AD trials to improve retention while controlling type I error and population drift.

nodes.text:
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper-b contributes a review of adaptive clinical trial designs, classifying them as prospective, concurrent (ad hoc), or retrospective. It identifies key risks: post-adaptation patient populations may drift from the original target population, uncontrolled type I error, and on-going trials that can no longer answer the original scientific/medical questions. It also discusses strategies for rare diseases and provides examples from Velcade trials in multiple myeloma and non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Cannot be specified. Only one source paper is available; the second paper’s method, concept, theory, or data contribution is missing. A genuine integration mechanism requires knowing what the second paper contributes, so no causal or operational connection can be proposed without inventing source results.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Cannot be specified. A testable study requires measurements and validation that combine both papers’ concrete contributions. With paper-b alone, only adaptive trial simulation or type I error monitoring could be designed, but that would not integrate a second discipline or paper.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
Unavailable. A compact abstract of an integrated project cannot be written without the second source paper’s contribution. Any abstract would either ignore the integration requirement or fabricate missing cross-paper knowledge.

FINAL IDEA: A genuine two-paper interdisciplinary proposal cannot be generated from the available material because the second source paper is missing; only the adaptive clinical trial design review is available, so any integration would be invented rather than grounded in the provided sources.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Adopt from Researcher B the paper-c claims: in an AD trial conjoint study (N=108 study partners), home visits had highest utility (0.89), offsetting high intervention risk disutility (−0.85); car service was redundant; home visits raised predicted willingness from 17% to 27%; low risk and higher chance of active treatment raised willingness to 60%; travel-hassle utility correlated with patient severity (ADL r=0.41, p<0.001; basic ADL r=0.38; NPI r=0.24; distress r=0.23) but not caregiver burden.  
Adopt paper-b’s adaptive design framework: prospective, concurrent/ ad hoc, and retrospective adaptations; concern that adaptations may shift the enrolled population away from the target and inflate type I error.  
Reject Researcher B’s “cannot integrate” conclusion because paper-b is now available. Reject Researcher C’s no-source stance; qualify both by noting the missing piece was a second paper’s concrete mechanism, now supplied by paper-c.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Use paper-c’s preference utilities to operationalize a prospective adaptive rule in paper-b’s framework. At interim analysis, if enrollment or retention of higher-severity patients (e.g., above median ADL) falls below target, pre-specify adding home visits. The rule connects causally: home-visit utility offsets travel/high risk disutility, predicted to raise willingness from 17% to 27% without adding likely redundant car service. Paper-b supplies type I error control for this pre-planned adaptation; paper-c supplies the utility weights that define when and how to adapt.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Simulation of a two-stage AD trial. Stage 1: standard site visits. At interim, apply the adaptive rule using paper-c utilities: if high-severity enrollment rate is below target or travel-related dropout is high, offer home visits in stage 2. Comparator arms: no adaptation; ad hoc home-visit addition; prospective home-visit rule; prospective rule plus covariate-adjusted randomization. Measurements: enrollment rate, retention, baseline ADL/NPI distribution pre- vs. post-adaptation (population drift), type I error under null via 10,000 simulations, power. Validation: benchmark simulated enrollment against paper-c predicted 17%→27% shift; confirm nominal type I error; sensitivity analyses varying home-visit and risk utilities. This tests whether preference-informed adaptation improves recruitment without population drift or error inflation.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
This project integrates adaptive trial design and AD trial preference data to test whether a pre-specified, preference-informed rule—adding home visits if severe-patient enrollment lags—improves recruitment/retention while controlling population drift and type I error. Simulation benchmarks against observed conjoint utilities and validates statistical properties.

FINAL IDEA: Use patient/study-partner preference utilities for home visits to define a prospective adaptive trial rule that adds home visits when interim data show under-enrollment of higher-severity AD patients, then test whether this adaptation improves recruitment without shifting the target population or inflating type I error.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Adopt paper-b’s adaptive design framework: prospective, concurrent/ad hoc, retrospective adaptations; risks of post-adaptation drift from the target population, uncontrolled type I error, and loss of answerability. Adopt paper-c claims as reported by colleagues: home-visit utility 0.89 offsets high-risk disutility −0.85; predicted willingness rises 17%→27%; travel-hassle utility correlates with severity (ADL r=0.41, p<0.001; basic ADL r=0.38; NPI r=0.24) but not caregiver burden. Qualify: paper-b is not AD-specific; paper-c is not adaptive. Reject Researcher B’s implication that home-visit adaptation necessarily causes harmful drift—paper-b allows pre-specified prospective rules to preserve the target population.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Treat adaptive amendments as preference-relevant trial attributes. Paper-c utilities specify how changing attributes (adding home visits, altering risk or active-treatment chance) shifts predicted enrollment by severity. Causal path: adaptation alters attribute levels → utility-weighted choice → severity-dependent enrollment/retention → paper-b population drift and type I error risk. Direction: higher severity increases travel-hassle disutility reduction, so home-visit adaptation should preferentially retain/recruit higher-severity dyads. This can correct under-enrollment if severe AD is targeted, or cause bias if the target is mild.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Build discrete-choice enrollment simulation using paper-c utilities. Design a two-arm AD trial with baseline site visits. Pre-specify prospective rule: at interim, if severe ADL/NPI stratum enrollment is below target, add home visits only for remaining recruitment. Comparator arms: no adaptation; ad hoc home-visit addition; car service; increased active-treatment chance. Outcomes: post-adaptation drift in severity distribution, type I error under null (10,000 simulations), power. Validate externally: survey 150 new AD study partners with adaptive-scenario conjoint cards; compare predicted vs. actual willingness and 12-week recruitment/retention by severity. SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper B contributes a review of adaptive clinical trial designs, distinguishing prospective, concurrent/ad hoc, and retrospective adaptations. It reports that ongoing adaptations can alter the actual patient population, shift trial objectives, and threaten type I error control. It also discusses rare-disease strategies, protocol amendment pitfalls, and examples including Velcade in multiple myeloma and non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

Paper A: not available in the supplied materials. Its title, abstract, methods, and actual claims are missing.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Cannot be specified without Paper A. A valid integration requires a concrete operational contribution from Paper A—such as a statistical estimation method, modeling framework, or measurement procedure—that can connect causally to Paper B’s population-drift and type-I-error problem. Shared keywords would not suffice, and I will not invent Paper A’s contribution.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Conditional only. If Paper A supplied a method for measuring or adjusting population drift, I would propose a simulation study linking that method to Paper B’s adaptation typology, quantifying type I error and interpretability after prospective versus ad hoc adaptations. At present, no testable measurements or validation can be responsibly specified.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
This proposal cannot be completed from the available sources. Paper B establishes the clinical-trial adaptation risks and design categories. The second source contribution is absent, so no genuine interdisciplinary mechanism or empirical design can be formulated without fabricating missing material.

FINAL IDEA: The integrated research idea cannot yet be stated because only Paper B is available; a non-fabricated integration requires the missing contribution from Paper A.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper B (available) contributes the adaptive-design taxonomy—prospective, concurrent/ad hoc, retrospective—and the specific warning that adaptation can shift the actual enrolled population, alter scientific objectives, and threaten type I error control.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b claims explicit constructions of linear complementary pairs (LCP) of algebraic geometry codes from elliptic curves, conditions under which \(C^\perp\) is equivalent to \(D\), and study of security parameters \(d(C), d(D^\perp)\); it also investigates MDS LCP AG codes.
- Paper-c claims characterizations of constacyclic and quasicyclic LCP codes, extends the Yang–Massey LCD cyclic criterion, and observes that for constacyclic LCP, \(D^\perp\) is equivalent to \(C\), so the security parameter reduces to one distance; it gives binary examples with better parameters than known LCD codes.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use elliptic-curve automorphisms from paper-b to impose constacyclic/quasicyclic structure on AG code pairs. Proposed hypothesis: elliptic-curve AG LCP codes invariant under a cyclic automorphism can be realized as constacyclic or quasicyclic codes; then paper-c’s characterization applies to reduce \(d(D^\perp)\) to \(d(C)\). This cross-family dictionary is not stated in either source.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Select explicit elliptic-curve LCP pairs from paper-b with known divisors and automorphisms. Test whether the codes are constacyclic/quasicyclic by expressing codewords as polynomial modules under the automorphism shift and computing generator polynomials. Apply paper-c’s criteria to verify LCP and equivalence; compute \(d(C)\) and \(d(D^\perp)\), compare with paper-b’s AG minimum-distance bounds. Search parameters against paper-c’s programming bound tables. Validate in Magma/Sage over small finite fields. Missing cross-paper knowledge: an explicit AG-to-constacyclic/quasicyclic identification must be derived, as neither source provides it.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose connecting explicit elliptic-curve LCP algebraic geometry codes with constacyclic/quasicyclic LCP characterizations. Paper-b supplies AG constructions; paper-c supplies cyclic-family criteria. By identifying when elliptic AG code pairs are constacyclic/quasicyclic under curve automorphisms, we aim to reduce the security parameter \(\min(d(C), d(D^\perp))\) to one distance and generate LCP codes with parameters exceeding known LCD codes. The study tests this dictionary computationally, bridging AG and cyclic code families.

FINAL IDEA: Use elliptic-curve automorphisms to recast LCP algebraic geometry codes as constacyclic/quasicyclic codes, thereby applying cyclic-family characterizations to compute their security parameters exactly.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b constructs LCP algebraic geometry (AG) codes from elliptic curves, studies security parameter \(\min(d(C),d(D^\perp))\), and gives conditions for \(C^\perp\) to be equivalent to \(D\).
- Paper-c characterizes constacyclic and quasicyclic LCP codes; for constacyclic pairs, \(D^\perp\) is equivalent to \(C\), so one distance determines the security parameter.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
I adopt Researcher B’s subgroup-evaluation mechanism as the operational bridge: evaluate elliptic-curve AG codes on a translation-invariant subgroup \(G\subseteq E(\mathbb{F}_q)\). This makes the code generator shift-invariant under the group-law translation automorphism. I qualify this as a hypothesis, not a guaranteed constacyclicity: subgroup invariance can yield constacyclic or quasicyclic structure, but the exact eigenvalue/shift relation must be derived. I reject Researcher C’s one-way “filter” framing; instead, I propose a two-way dictionary: paper-b’s curve automorphisms supply symmetry, paper-c’s constacyclic characterizations classify which symmetric AG codes collapse to one distance.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Construct elliptic-curve LCP pairs \((C,D)\) over small \(\mathbb{F}_q\) using one-point AG codes on two divisors, then restrict evaluation sets to a cyclic subgroup \(G\). Check constacyclic/quasicyclic form via generator matrices and shift operators. Apply paper-c’s criterion to test whether \(D^\perp\sim C\); then compare \(d(C)\) and \(d(D^\perp)\). Search for MDS examples and compare with paper-c’s programming bound tables. Validate in SageMath/Magma. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no extant lemma links elliptic-curve subgroup evaluation sets to constacyclic/quasicyclic LCP structure; this must be proved or refuted computationally.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We connect elliptic-curve AG code symmetries with constacyclic/quasicyclic LCP characterizations. Using translation-invariant subgroup evaluation sets, we test whether LCP AG codes become constacyclic or quasicyclic. When paper-c’s equivalence \(D^\perp\sim C\) applies, the security parameter reduces to one distance, enabling systematic MDS LCP search. The contribution is a constructive symmetry dictionary bridging AG and cyclic-family code theory.

FINAL IDEA: Evaluate elliptic-curve LCP AG codes on translation-invariant subgroups and use constacyclic/quasicyclic characterizations to collapse their security parameter to a single minimum distance.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b constructs explicit LCP algebraic geometry (AG) codes from elliptic curves and studies security parameter \(\min(d(C),d(D^\perp))\).
- Paper-c characterizes constacyclic/quasicyclic LCP codes and shows that for constacyclic LCP, \(D^\perp\sim C\), reducing the security parameter to one distance.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Adopt Researcher B’s subgroup-evaluation link as the concrete bridge. Qualify it as a hypothesis: evaluating AG codes on a cyclic translation subgroup \(G\subset E(\mathbb{F}_q)\) may make them constacyclic, but neither paper proves this. Reject Researcher C’s one-way filtering as underspecified because constacyclicity must be explicitly constructed via the translation action. Proposed mechanism: use the elliptic-curve translation automorphism \(\tau\) on evaluation points. When \(G\) is \(\tau\)-invariant, define \(C,D\) from Riemann-Roch spaces shifted by a multiplier so that the codeword coordinate permutation is \(\lambda\)-constacyclic. Then paper-c’s constacyclic theorem forces \(D^\perp\sim C\), collapsing two distances to \(d(C)\).

RESEARCH DESIGN:
For small \(q\), select elliptic curves \(E/\mathbb{F}_q\) with cyclic rational subgroup \(G\) of order \(n\). Construct AG pairs \(C=\mathrm{ev}_G(V)\), \(D=\mathrm{ev}_G(W)\) using paper-b’s LCP strategy, choosing \(W\) as a multiplier shift of \(V\) to align with translation. Validate:
1. LCP: \(C\cap D^\perp=\{0\}\) and \(C+D^\perp=\mathbb{F}_q^n\).
2. Constacyclicity: write codewords as polynomial modules under \(\tau\); compute generator polynomial and test paper-c’s criterion for a nonzero constant \(\lambda\).
3. Verify \(D^\perp\sim C\) and compute \(d(C),d(D^\perp)\).
4. Compare against paper-c’s programming bound and search for MDS examples.
Use SageMath/Magma for \(q\le 64\). Missing cross-paper knowledge: no lemma links subgroup-evaluated elliptic AG codes to constacyclic LCP; this must be proved or refuted computationally.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose constructing constacyclic LCP algebraic geometry codes by evaluating Riemann-Roch spaces on cyclic translation subgroups of elliptic curves. If translation symmetry induces constacyclicity, paper-c’s dual-equivalence collapses the security parameter to one distance. We test the construction over small finite fields and search for MDS examples, bridging AG and constacyclic code theory.

FINAL IDEA: Evaluate elliptic-curve LCP algebraic geometry codes on cyclic translation subgroups to induce constacyclicity and use constacyclic dual-equivalence to reduce their security parameter to a single distance.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-b constructs explicit linear complementary pairs (LCP) of algebraic geometry (AG) codes from elliptic curves, studies security parameters \(d(\mathcal{C})\) and \(d(\mathcal{D}^\perp)\), gives conditions for \(\mathcal{C}^\perp\) to be equivalent to \(\mathcal{D}\), and investigates MDS LCP AG codes.
Paper-c characterizes constacyclic and quasi-cyclic LCP codes; for constacyclic pairs \((C,D)\), it shows \(D^\perp\) is equivalent to \(C\), so the security parameter reduces to a single minimum distance. It also provides binary examples with better parameters than known LCD codes.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use elliptic-curve AG code constructions from paper-b, but restrict evaluation sets and divisors to carry the constacyclic symmetry characterized in paper-c. Operationally, choose evaluation points as a subgroup of the elliptic curve’s group-law translation automorphisms; this makes the resulting AG codes constacyclic. Paper-c’s constacyclic equivalence then collapses the LCP security parameter to one distance, while paper-b’s elliptic-curve machinery supplies the algebraic construction and MDS parameter control.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Construct LCP pairs \((\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})\) on an elliptic curve \(E/\mathbb{F}_q\) using two Riemann-Roch spaces evaluated on a translation-invariant subgroup \(G\subset E(\mathbb{F}_q)\). Test constacyclicity by checking shift invariance under the induced permutation. Validate the LCP condition \(\mathcal{C}\cap \mathcal{D}^\perp = \{0\}\) and \(\mathcal{C}+\mathcal{D}^\perp = \mathbb{F}_q^n\). Use paper-c’s characterization to test \(\mathcal{D}^\perp \sim \mathcal{C}\). Compute \(d(\mathcal{C})\), \(d(\mathcal{D}^\perp)\), and compare the pair’s security parameter with known LCD/AG bounds. Search small \(q,n\) for MDS examples.

Missing cross-paper knowledge: no existing theorem guarantees that elliptic-curve AG codes on subgroup evaluation sets are constacyclic LCP; this must be established computationally and characterized.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose combining elliptic-curve AG code constructions with constacyclic LCP structure. By evaluating algebraic geometry codes on translation-invariant subgroups of elliptic curves, we obtain constacyclic LCP pairs whose security parameter collapses via the equivalence \(D^\perp \sim C\). We test this construction over small finite fields and search for MDS examples, connecting AG-code symmetry with constacyclic coding theory.

FINAL IDEA: Construct constacyclic linear complementary pairs of algebraic geometry codes from elliptic-curve subgroup evaluation sets, using constacyclic equivalence to reduce their security parameter to a single distance.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-b constructs explicit LCP algebraic geometry (AG) codes from elliptic curves, studies security parameter \(d(C),d(D^\perp)\), gives conditions for \(C^\perp\sim D\), and investigates MDS LCP AG codes.
Paper-c characterizes constacyclic/quasicyclic LCP codes and shows that for constacyclic pairs \(C,D\), \(D^\perp\sim C\), so one distance determines the security parameter.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Adopt paper-b’s elliptic-curve AG construction and paper-c’s constacyclic duality characterization. Reject any implicit claim that AG codes are already constacyclic; qualify colleagues A/C by requiring an explicit translation-induced shift. Hypothesis: if the elliptic curve has a cyclic translation subgroup \(G=\langle \tau\rangle\) and Riemann-Roch divisors are chosen with translation symmetry, then the resulting AG pair is \(\lambda\)-constacyclic under \(\tau\), so paper-c’s dual-equivalence theorem applies.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Fix \(E/\mathbb{F}_q\) with rational cyclic subgroup \(G\) of order \(n\). Define \(C=\mathrm{ev}_G(V)\), \(D=\mathrm{ev}_G(W)\), where \(V,W\) are Riemann-Roch spaces such that \(W\) is a multiplier shift of \(V\). Validate LCP via \(C\cap D^\perp=\{0\}\) and \(C+D^\perp=\mathbb{F}_q^n\). Validate constacyclicity by checking \((\tau(c))_i=\lambda c_{i+1}\) for all \(c\). Then use paper-c’s equivalence \(D^\perp\sim C\) and compare measured \(d(C),d(D^\perp)\). Search small \(q,n\) in SageMath for MDS parameters. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source proves translation-invariant AG codes are constacyclic; this requires a new lemma.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose constructing constacyclic LCP algebraic geometry codes by evaluating Riemann-Roch spaces on cyclic translation subgroups of elliptic curves. If translation symmetry induces constacyclicity, paper-c’s dual-equivalence result collapses the security parameter to one distance. We test this computationally over small finite fields and search for MDS examples, bridging AG and constacyclic coding theory.

FINAL IDEA: Use elliptic-curve translation subgroups to build constacyclic LCP algebraic geometry codes and apply constacyclic duality to reduce the two-distance security parameter to one testable distance.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-b constructs explicit LCP algebraic geometry (AG) codes from elliptic curves, gives conditions for \(C^\perp\sim D\), studies \(d(C),d(D^\perp)\), and searches for MDS LCP AG codes.
Paper-c characterizes constacyclic/quasi-cyclic LCP codes and shows that for constacyclic LCP, \(D^\perp\sim C\), reducing the security parameter to one distance.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Adopt paper-b’s elliptic-curve AG LCP machinery but confine evaluation sets to a cyclic subgroup \(G=\langle P\rangle\subset E(\mathbb{F}_q)\). Adopt paper-c’s constacyclic duality theorem. Qualify colleagues A and C: subgroup evaluation alone does not guarantee constacyclic structure; it may yield quasi-cyclic or block-cyclic codes. The missing condition is a scalar action of the translation automorphism \(\tau:G\to G\) on the Riemann-Roch space, such that \(\tau(c)_i=\lambda c_{i+1}\). This makes the pair \(\lambda\)-constacyclic. Reject any one-way filtering without checking this scalar action.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Fix \(E/\mathbb{F}_q\) with a point \(P\) of order \(n\), set \(G=\langle P\rangle\), choose \(\tau\)-invariant divisors \(A,B\). Construct \(C=\mathrm{ev}_G(L(A))\), \(D=\mathrm{ev}_G(L(B))\). Test LCP: \(C\cap D^\perp=\{0\}\) and \(C+D^\perp=\mathbb{F}_q^n\). Test constacyclicity by computing the action of \(\tau\) on the basis of \(L(A)\); if it acts as a scalar \(\lambda\), verify codeword shift relation. Apply paper-c’s criterion to check \(D^\perp\sim C\). Compute \(d(C),d(D^\perp)\), compare with paper-b’s MDS conditions and paper-c’s programming bound. Search \(q\le 64\) in SageMath/Magma. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source proves scalar translation action yields \(\lambda\)-constacyclic AG codes; this requires a new lemma.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose constructing \(\lambda\)-constacyclic LCP algebraic geometry codes by evaluating Riemann-Roch spaces on cyclic translation subgroups of elliptic curves and requiring a scalar translation action. Paper-b supplies AG LCP construction; paper-c supplies constacyclic duality. If the scalar-action hypothesis holds, the security parameter collapses to one distance, enabling systematic MDS LCP search.

FINAL IDEA: Evaluate elliptic-curve AG LCP codes on cyclic subgroups with a scalar translation action, yielding \(\lambda\)-constacyclic LCP pairs whose security parameter collapses via paper-c’s constacyclic duality theorem.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b: First study of LCP algebraic geometry codes; constructs explicit LCP codes from elliptic curves; uses security parameter \(\min(d(C), d(D^\perp))\); shows \(C^\perp\) equivalent to \(D\) under specific conditions; investigates MDS LCP AG codes.
- Paper-c: Characterizes constacyclic and quasi-cyclic LCP codes; extends Yang-Massey LCD cyclic characterization; proves that for constacyclic LCP, \(D^\perp\) is equivalent to \(C\), so one distance determines the security parameter; provides binary LCP examples and programming bound tables.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use paper-c’s constacyclic/quasi-cyclic LCP characterizations as an algebraic filter on paper-b’s elliptic-curve AG code constructions. The proposed causal link: if elliptic-curve AG LCP pairs can be built with constacyclic/quasi-cyclic symmetry, then paper-c’s dual-equivalence result collapses paper-b’s two-distance security parameter to one computable distance, making MDS LCP search efficient. This link is a hypothesis, not established in either source.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Construct LCP AG code pairs from elliptic curves over small finite fields using paper-b’s method. Test whether the pairs satisfy paper-c’s constacyclic/quasi-cyclic criteria via automorphism groups and generator-matrix structure. Measure: direct-sum LCP condition, \(d(C)\), \(d(D^\perp)\), and equivalence \(C^\perp \sim D\). Compare resulting minimum distances to paper-c’s programming bound and table. Validate computationally in SageMath/Magma. Missing cross-paper knowledge: exact sufficient conditions for an elliptic-curve AG code to be constacyclic or quasi-cyclic; this requires a new lemma.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose bridging constacyclic/quasi-cyclic LCP coding theory with algebraic geometry code construction. Starting from explicit elliptic-curve LCP AG codes, we screen for pairs with constacyclic/quasi-cyclic symmetry. If found, paper-c’s dual-equivalence theorem reduces the security parameter to one distance, enabling systematic search for MDS LCP AG codes. The contribution is a constructive method linking algebraic code symmetries to curve-based LCP security parameters.

FINAL IDEA: Use constacyclic/quasi-cyclic LCP characterizations to filter elliptic-curve algebraic geometry LCP constructions, collapsing the two-distance security parameter and enabling efficient MDS LCP search.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b: explicit LCP algebraic geometry (AG) codes from elliptic curves; conditions for \(C^\perp\sim D\); security parameter \(\min(d(C),d(D^\perp))\); MDS LCP AG search.
- Paper-c: constacyclic/quasi-cyclic LCP characterizations; for constacyclic LCP, \(D^\perp\sim C\), reducing security parameter to one distance.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Adopt Researcher B’s subgroup evaluation-set idea as the concrete link. Paper-b’s elliptic-curve AG codes become constacyclic when evaluation points form a subgroup \(G\subset E(\mathbb{F}_q)\) invariant under a translation automorphism. Paper-c’s constacyclic theorem then forces \(D^\perp\sim C\), so \(\min(d(C),d(D^\perp))=d(C)\). Qualify Researcher A: curve automorphisms alone do not guarantee a constacyclic representation; a subgroup orbit is the missing constructive condition. Reject broad “filtering” as underspecified without checking the subgroup structure.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
For small \(q\), choose elliptic curves \(E/\mathbb{F}_q\) with translation automorphism \(\tau\). Let \(G\subseteq E(\mathbb{F}_q)\) be a \(\tau\)-orbit/subgroup. Construct AG code pairs \(C=C_\mathcal{L}(A,G)\), \(D=C_\mathcal{L}(B,G)\) using two divisors \(A,B\) supported on \(G\), following paper-b’s LCP construction. Test:
1. LCP condition \(C\cap D^\perp=\{0\}\), \(C+D^\perp=\mathbb{F}_q^n\).
2. Constacyclicity: represent codewords as polynomial modules under \(\tau\); compute generator polynomials and apply paper-c’s criteria.
3. Verify \(D^\perp\sim C\) and compute \(d(C)\), \(d(D^\perp)\).
4. Compare against paper-c’s programming bound and paper-b’s MDS criteria.
Validate in Magma for \(q\le 64\). Missing cross-paper knowledge: no theorem from either source proves subgroup-evaluated elliptic AG pairs are constacyclic LCP; this must be established as a lemma.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose constructing constacyclic LCP codes from elliptic-curve AG codes by evaluating on translation-invariant subgroups. Paper-b supplies AG LCP machinery; paper-c supplies constacyclic characterization. If subgroup-evaluated pairs satisfy paper-c’s condition, the security parameter collapses to \(d(C)\), enabling systematic MDS LCP search and bridging AG and constacyclic code theories.

FINAL IDEA: Evaluate elliptic-curve algebraic geometry LCP codes on translation-invariant subgroups to force constacyclic structure, then use paper-c’s equivalence theorem to reduce the security parameter to one distance and search for MDS examples.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b: explicit LCP algebraic geometry (AG) codes from elliptic curves; conditions for \(C^\perp\sim D\); security parameter \(\min(d(C),d(D^\perp))\); MDS LCP search.
- Paper-c: constacyclic/quasicyclic LCP characterizations; for constacyclic pairs, \(D^\perp\sim C\), so one distance determines the security parameter.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Adopt Researcher B’s subgroup-evaluation mechanism: paper-b’s elliptic-curve group-law translation subgroup \(G=\langle\tau\rangle\) induces a cyclic shift on evaluation coordinates; if Riemann-Roch divisors are translation-invariant, the AG pair may become \(\lambda\)-constacyclic. Qualify Researcher A: curve automorphism alone is insufficient; the explicit shift condition under \(\tau\) is required. Reject any source claim that AG codes are already constacyclic/quasicyclic without this construction. Operational link: paper-b supplies the elliptic-curve LCP construction and MDS parameters; paper-c supplies the constacyclic dual-equivalence theorem that collapses \(\min(d(C),d(D^\perp))\) to \(d(C)\).

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Use paper-b’s explicit elliptic-curve LCP construction but require evaluation set to be a cyclic subgroup \(G\subseteq E(\mathbb{F}_q)\) of order \(n\). Choose divisors \(A,B\) invariant under translation by \(G\). Validate constacyclicity by checking \((\tau(c))_i=\lambda c_{i+1}\) for all codewords \(c\), via shift-operator matrices and generator polynomials. Test LCP: \(C\cap D^\perp=\{0\}\) and \(C+D^\perp=\mathbb{F}_q^n\). Apply paper-c’s criterion to verify \(D^\perp\sim C\), then compute \(d(C)\), \(d(D^\perp)\) and compare with paper-c’s programming bound and paper-b’s MDS existence question. Search \(q\le 64\), small \(n\) in SageMath/Magma. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no theorem from either paper proves translation-invariant elliptic AG pairs are constacyclic LCP; this lemma must be established or refuted computationally.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose testing whether elliptic-curve LCP AG codes evaluated on translation-invariant subgroups become constacyclic. If validated, paper-c’s dual-equivalence collapses the security parameter to one distance, enabling systematic MDS LCP search and bridging algebraic geometry and constacyclic coding theory.

FINAL IDEA: Evaluate elliptic-curve LCP algebraic geometry codes on translation-invariant cyclic subgroups, test their constacyclicity, and use paper-c’s dual-equivalence to reduce the security parameter to one computable distance for MDS search.

Title: On linear complementary pairs of algebraic geometry codes over finite fields
Abstract: Linear complementary dual (LCD) codes and linear complementary pairs (LCP) of codes have been proposed for new applications as countermeasures against side-channel attacks (SCA) and fault injection attacks (FIA) in the context of direct sum masking (DSM). The countermeasure against FIA may lead to a vulnerability for SCA when the whole algorithm needs to be masked (in environments like smart cards). This led to a variant of the LCD and LCP problems, where several results have been obtained intensively for LCD codes, but only partial results have been derived for LCP codes. Given the gap between the thin results and their particular importance, this paper aims to reduce this by further studying the LCP of codes in special code families and, precisely, the characterisation and construction mechanism of LCP codes of algebraic geometry codes over finite fields. Notably, we propose constructing explicit LCP of codes from elliptic curves. Besides, we also study the security parameters of the derived LCP of codes $(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{D})$ (notably for cyclic codes), which are given by the minimum distances $d(\mathcal{C})$ and $d(\mathcal{D}^\perp)$. Further, we show that for LCP algebraic geometry codes $(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})$, the dual code $\mathcal{C}^\perp$ is equivalent to $\mathcal{D}$ under some specific conditions we exhibit. Finally, we investigate whether MDS LCP of algebraic geometry codes exist (MDS codes are among the most important in coding theory due to their theoretical significance and practical interests). Construction schemes for obtaining LCD codes from any algebraic curve were given in 2018 by Mesnager, Tang and Qi in [``Complementary dual algebraic geometry codes", IEEE Trans. Inform Theory, vol. 64(4), 2390--3297, 2018]. To our knowledge, it is the first time LCP of algebraic geometry codes has been studied.
