papers.text:
Title: Phase Diagram of the Ashkin-Teller Model
Abstract: The Ashkin-Teller model is a pair of interacting Ising models and has two parameters: J is a coupling constant in the Ising models and U describes the strength of the interaction between them. In the ferromagnetic case J,U>0 on the square lattice, we establish a complete phase diagram conjectured in physics in 1970s (by Kadanoff and Wegner, Wu and Lin, Baxter and others): when J<U, the transitions for the Ising spins and their products occur at two distinct curves that are dual to each other; when J\geq U, both transitions occur at the self-dual curve. All transitions are shown to be sharp using the OSSS inequality. We use a finite-criterion argument and continuity to extend the result of Peled and the third author \cite{GlaPel19} from a self-dual point to its neighborhood. Our proofs go through the random-cluster representation of the Ashkin-Teller model introduced by Chayes-Machta and Pfister-Velenik and we rely on couplings to FK-percolation.

Title: On critical properties of the Ashkin-Teller model
Abstract: The critical properties of the Ashkin-Teller model in the special case where two pair energies are the same are shown to be the same as those of the eight-vertex model in the weak-coupling limit as a consequence of scaling hypothesis.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- paper-b: PCLR uses contrastive pretraining on 3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs to create expressive representations, improving downstream tasks with fewer than 5,000 labels.
- paper-c: A supervised CNN trained on paired ECG-echocardiogram data identifies ALVD (EF≤35%) from ECG alone, with AUC 0.93 and 4.1× future dysfunction risk for screen-positive patients.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
PCLR provides a self-supervised ECG encoder that reduces dependence on labeled echocardiograms; paper-c provides the clinical contractile phenotype and paired ECG-echo validation framework. Operationally, the PCLR encoder is fine-tuned or linearly probed with limited EF labels, using EF≤35% as the target.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Use PCLR pretrained on large unlabeled 12-lead ECGs. Obtain paired ECG-echo data similar to paper-c (n≈44,959) with left ventricular ejection fraction. Create training subsets of 500, 1,000, 2,000, and 5,000 labeled patients. Compare PCLR linear probe/fine-tuning against a de novo CNN matching paper-c’s architecture on identical subsets. Test on an independent set; measure AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy for EF≤35%, and calibration. In test patients with baseline EF>35%, follow longitudinally and estimate hazard ratio for incident EF≤35% between positive and negative screens. Validate on a held-out temporal split or external site.

Missing cross-paper knowledge: paper-b did not test echocardiographic phenotypes; paper-c did not use contrastive pretraining; no evidence yet that PCLR embeddings transfer to contractile dysfunction labels.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose integrating contrastive self-supervised ECG representation learning with AI-enabled contractile dysfunction screening. PCLR pretraining on millions of unlabeled ECGs will be fine-tuned on limited paired ECG-echocardiogram labels to identify asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction. We hypothesize this improves low-label screening accuracy and preserves prognostic risk stratification, yielding a label-efficient, clinically practical screening tool.

FINAL IDEA: Self-supervised PCLR pretraining will be combined with echocardiogram-defined contractile dysfunction labels to create a label-efficient ECG screening model for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- paper-b: PCLR contrastively pretrains on 3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs to create reusable representations, improving downstream tasks with <5,000 labels.
- paper-c: paired ECG-echo CNN detects ALVD (LVEF≤35%) from ECG alone, AUC 0.93, and a positive screen predicts 4.1× hazard for future dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Adopt paper-b’s self-supervised encoder as a label-efficient feature extractor and paper-c’s clinically validated outcome (LVEF≤35%) and prognostic link. Qualify both prior proposals: they assume PCLR features transfer to contractile dysfunction without evidence. Therefore the operational mechanism is two-stage: first test whether PCLR embeddings linearly predict continuous echocardiographic LVEF; only if this passes, fine-tune a binary screening head for EF≤35. This causally connects representation quality to the screening target before deployment.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Use paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data from one institution plus an external site. Pretrain PCLR on all unlabeled ECGs. Freeze encoder; train Ridge regression to predict continuous LVEF and logistic regression for EF≤35 on 500, 1,000, 2,000, and 5,000 labeled pairs. Compare against paper-c-style supervised CNN and against PCLR linear probe. Metrics: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration; for patients with baseline EF>35, estimate hazard ratio for incident EF≤35 by screen status. Validate temporally and externally. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source evidence that PCLR embeddings encode LVEF; therefore continuous-probe step is required, not optional.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose to test whether PCLR’s self-supervised ECG representations transfer to echocardiographic contractile function before building a label-efficient ALVD screen. Using paired ECGs and continuous LVEF, we first assess linear predictability of PCLR embeddings for systolic function, then fine-tune for EF≤35 at label fractions as low as 500. Success would decouple ALVD screening from large echo-labeled training sets and clarify whether contrastive ECG representations capture structural cardiac information.

FINAL IDEA: PCLR self-supervised ECG embeddings must first linearly predict continuous LVEF before being fine-tuned for EF≤35, making ALVD screening label-efficient and mechanistically validated.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- paper-b: PCLR contrastively pretrains on 3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs, improving downstream tasks with <5,000 labels. Adopt encoder; qualify: no echo/LVEF validation in source.
- paper-c: supervised CNN on paired ECG-echo detects EF≤35 with AUC 0.93 and 4.1× hazard. Adopt EF≤35 as clinical target and paired echo validation; reject direct use of its trained weights; qualify generalizability and label efficiency untested.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Reject both colleagues’ implicit assumption that PCLR can be fine-tuned directly for ALVD without checking transfer. Instead use a two-stage causal bridge: first test whether frozen PCLR embeddings linearly predict continuous LVEF from echocardiograms; only if this passes, attach a logistic head for EF≤35 and optionally low-rank fine-tune. This makes paper-c’s continuous ejection fraction the mechanistic validation that PCLR representations actually encode contractile function before building the binary screen.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Use paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data, temporally split with an external site. Pretrain PCLR on unlabeled ECGs from both sites. Stage 1: ridge regression from frozen PCLR embeddings to continuous LVEF using 500, 1,000, 2,500, and 5,000 paired labels; report R² and calibration. Stage 2: if Stage 1 shows nonzero LVEF variance explained, train logistic head for EF≤35 on same label splits; compare frozen PCLR probe, low-rank fine-tuned PCLR, and de novo paper-c-style CNN. Metrics: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration; in patients with baseline EF>35, estimate hazard ratio for incident EF≤35 by screen status. Validate externally and test noninferiority to paper-c’s fully supervised AUC 0.93.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We test whether PCLR’s self-supervised ECG representations encode continuous left ventricular ejection fraction before building a label-efficient ALVD screen. Stage 1 probes frozen PCLR against continuous LVEF; Stage 2 fine-tunes for EF≤35 only if transfer succeeds. This validates cross-modal representation transfer and creates an externally validated, low-label screening tool with prognostic utility.

FINAL IDEA: PCLR self-supervised ECG embeddings must first linearly predict continuous LVEF before being used for EF≤35, ensuring contractile-dysfunction transfer and enabling label-efficient, externally validated ALVD screening.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b: PCLR provides a self-supervised contrastive pre-training method that learns ECG representations from 3.2 million unlabeled 12-lead ECGs and improves downstream clinical tasks with fewer than 5,000 labels.
- Paper-c: Demonstrates a supervised CNN using paired ECG-echocardiogram data can screen asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD; ejection fraction ≤35%) with AUC 0.93, and a positive AI screen predicts future ventricular dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use PCLR’s pre-trained ECG encoder as the feature extractor for the ALVD screening task from paper-c. Contrastive pre-training supplies a rich, label-efficient representation; paper-c supplies the clinically validated outcome definition and screening framework. The operational connection is fine-tuning PCLR on small labeled ECG-echocardiogram pairs. Missing cross-paper knowledge: PCLR was not evaluated for ALVD or echo-derived ejection fraction, and paper-c did not use self-supervised pre-training; whether PCLR embeddings retain contractile-dysfunction information is unknown.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Obtain an external cohort with paired 12-lead ECGs and echocardiograms. Pre-train PCLR on unlabeled ECGs from the same institution, then fine-tune for EF≤35 using only 500, 1,000, and 5,000 labeled ECG-echo pairs. Compare against a from-scratch CNN matching paper-c and a linear probe on frozen PCLR features. Measure AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and calibration on held-out echo labels; additionally follow screen-positive patients without baseline dysfunction to estimate hazard ratio for incident ALVD. Validate across at least two sites.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We integrate self-supervised ECG representation learning with echocardiogram-defined ALVD screening to reduce labeled-data requirements. PCLR representations are fine-tuned on small ECG-echo cohorts and benchmarked against a supervised CNN. The study tests whether contrastive pre-training preserves contractile-dysfunction signals and improves low-label screening performance, enabling scalable ALVD detection with limited echo labels.

FINAL IDEA: Fine-tuning PCLR’s contrastively pre-trained ECG representations on small ECG-echocardiogram cohorts can make paper-c’s ALVD screening more label-efficient and broadly deployable.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b: PCLR learns self-supervised 12-lead ECG representations from 3.2M unlabeled ECGs and improves downstream tasks with fewer than 5,000 labels.
- Paper-c: A supervised CNN on paired ECG-echocardiogram data detects asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF≤35%) from ECG alone with AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, and a 4.1× hazard for future dysfunction in screen-positive patients.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Adopt PCLR’s contrastive pretraining as encoder, but qualify that its transfer to echocardiographic LVEF is untested. Adopt paper-c’s EF≤35% as clinical target. Operational link: fine-tune PCLR on small ECG-echo labeled sets, hypothesizing that contrastive ECG features encode contractile-dysfunction-relevant morphology and reduce label dependence. Reject any claim that PCLR already solves ALVD screening without echo validation.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Use PCLR pretrained on unlabeled 12-lead ECGs. Cohort: paired ECGs and echocardiograms with LVEF. Train on 500, 1,000, 2,500, and 5,000 labeled patients; compare fine-tuned PCLR, linear probe on frozen PCLR, and a de novo CNN matching paper-c. Primary: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration for LVEF≤35% on independent test. Secondary: in test patients with baseline LVEF>35%, estimate hazard ratio for incident LVEF≤35% by screen status. External validation at a separate center; test noninferiority to paper-c’s supervised CNN trained on 44,959 labels. Missing cross-paper knowledge: whether PCLR embeddings align with LVEF and the minimum label threshold remain proposed hypotheses.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We test whether self-supervised ECG contrastive representations reduce the labeled echocardiogram burden for AI screening of asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction. PCLR is fine-tuned or linearly probed on small ECG-echo cohorts and compared with a supervised CNN, assessing accuracy and future dysfunction risk. Success would extend PCLR’s label efficiency to functional cardiac screening while preserving paper-c’s prognostic value.

FINAL IDEA: Fine-tune PCLR’s self-supervised ECG representations on limited ECG-echo labels to achieve label-efficient, externally validated screening for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction, bridging contrastive ECG learning and echocardiogram-defined contractile dysfunction.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- paper-b: PCLR pre-trains contrastively on 3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs, improving downstream tasks with <5,000 labels.
- paper-c: Supervised CNN on paired ECG-echo detects ALVD (LVEF≤35%) from ECG alone, AUC 0.93; positive screen carries 4.1× hazard for future dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Adopt paper-b’s frozen PCLR encoder and paper-c’s clinical target EF≤35 plus prognostic validation. Adopt Researcher A’s two-stage transfer check; reject automatic transfer of contrastive features to contractile dysfunction and reject direct reuse of paper-c’s trained weights. Qualify: PCLR’s expressiveness is not evidence for LVEF-relevant structure. Operationally, PCLR embeddings must first linearly predict continuous LVEF via Ridge regression; only then fine-tune for EF≤35. This conservative gating couples representation quality to the clinical outcome before deployment.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Use paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram cohort from one institution plus independent external site. Pre-train PCLR on all unlabeled ECGs. Stage 1: frozen PCLR features predict continuous LVEF; require validation Pearson r≥0.70. Stage 2: on 500/1,000/2,500/5,000 labeled pairs, train logistic head or light fine-tune for EF≤35; compare frozen linear probe, fine-tuned PCLR, and de novo CNN (paper-c architecture). Evaluate AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration; in baseline LVEF>35 patients, estimate hazard ratio for incident EF≤35. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source shows PCLR encodes LVEF; the r≥0.70 threshold is proposed.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We test whether self-supervised PCLR ECG representations transfer to echocardiographic function before using them for label-efficient ALVD screening. A two-stage design first linearly probes continuous LVEF, then fine-tunes for EF≤35 at low label counts, with external and longitudinal validation. Success would show contrastive ECG features retain contractile information and reduce echo-label burden.

FINAL IDEA: PCLR self-supervised ECG representations must first linearly predict continuous LVEF before fine-tuning for EF≤35, enabling label-efficient, externally validated ALVD screening only if contractile information is preserved.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-b: PCLR learns latent 12-lead ECG representations via contrastive pre-training on 3.2 million unlabeled ECGs and improves downstream clinical tasks with fewer than 5,000 labels.
Paper-c: A supervised CNN trained on 44,959 paired ECG-echocardiograms detects asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF ≤35%) from ECG alone, reporting AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, and a 4.1 hazard ratio for future dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use PCLR’s self-supervised ECG encoder as a frozen feature extractor or fine-tuned initialization for a lightweight ALVD classifier. The operational link is transfer of unlabeled ECG representations to reduce the number of expensive paired echocardiogram labels needed for contractile-dysfunction screening.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Cohort: de-identified 12-lead ECGs with paired echocardiograms and LVEF. Train PCLR encoder + linear/logistic head on small labeled sets of 500, 1,000, 2,500, and 5,000 patients. Baseline: de novo CNN from paper-c trained on the same small sets; linear probe of PCLR. Measure AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration, and hazard ratio for future dysfunction in initially screen-negative patients. Validate on temporally separated or external ECGs. Compare against paper-c’s reported fully supervised performance.

Missing cross-paper knowledge: Neither paper reports whether PCLR representations align with echocardiographic LVEF labels; transferability and minimum label requirements are proposed hypotheses, not source findings.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose testing whether self-supervised contrastive ECG representations from PCLR can lower the labeled echocardiogram burden for AI screening of asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction. Using PCLR with small ECG-echo training sets, we will evaluate noninferiority to a fully supervised CNN trained on 44,959 pairs. This could extend low-label ECG modeling to structural/functional cardiac screening and clarify whether contrastive ECG features transfer to LVEF prediction.

FINAL IDEA: Integrating PCLR self-supervised ECG pretraining with supervised ECG-echocardiogram screening to test whether contrastive ECG representations enable accurate detection of asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction with far fewer labeled echocardiograms than a de novo CNN.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- paper-b: PCLR provides a self-supervised contrastive ECG encoder trained on 3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs, improving low-label downstream tasks.
- paper-c: Supervised CNN on paired ECG-echocardiogram data detects ALVD (EF≤35%) with AUC 0.93, and positive screens carry a 4.1× hazard for future dysfunction.

Adopt: PCLR as representation learner; EF≤35 as target; small labeled subcohorts; longitudinal hazard validation. Reject: using paper-c’s trained CNN weights directly; we replicate architecture only. Qualify: paper-b never tested contractile-dysfunction labels, and paper-c never used self-supervised pretraining; PCLR’s “expressive” claim is not evidence it retains LVEF-relevant structure.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Frozen PCLR patient embeddings are mapped by a linear head to predict EF≤35. Optionally, low-rank fine-tuning adapts the encoder. The operational connection is that contrastive ECG representations supply label-efficient features, while echocardiogram-defined EF≤35 supplies the clinical outcome.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
External cohort with paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram. Pre-train PCLR on unlabeled ECGs. Train on 500/1,000/2,500/5,000 labeled pairs. Compare frozen PCLR linear probe, fine-tuned PCLR, and de novo CNN. Measure AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration; estimate hazard ratio for incident EF≤35 among initially screen-negative patients. Validate on temporal split or second site.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We test whether PCLR contrastive ECG representations identify asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction with limited echocardiogram labels. Frozen and fine-tuned PCLR are benchmarked against a de novo CNN on paired ECG-echo data, including future dysfunction risk. This can establish label-efficient transfer from ECG self-supervision to structural cardiac screening.

FINAL IDEA: Self-supervised PCLR ECG embeddings, linearly probed or fine-tuned with small echocardiogram-labeled cohorts, may match supervised ALVD screening while reducing the labeled echo burden if contrastive representations preserve LVEF-relevant information.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- paper-b: PCLR contrastively pretrains on 3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs and improves downstream tasks with <5,000 labels.
- paper-c: Supervised CNN on paired ECG-echo detects LVEF≤35 from ECG alone; AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, and 4.1× hazard for future dysfunction.
Adopt: PCLR encoder, echo-defined EF≤35, prognostic validation. Reject: assumption that PCLR directly transfers to contractile dysfunction without testing. Qualify: PCLR’s “expressive” claim does not guarantee LVEF-relevant embeddings.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Two-stage. First test whether frozen PCLR embeddings linearly predict continuous LVEF via Ridge regression and binary EF≤35 via logistic probe. Only if both show above-chance prediction on limited labels do we fine-tune the encoder. This operational link uses paper-c’s echocardiographic labels as the downstream clinical signal and paper-b’s self-supervised ECG encoder as the label-efficient feature source.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Use an external paired ECG-echo cohort. Pretrain PCLR on unlabeled ECGs. Train on 500/1,000/2,500/5,000 labeled pairs. Compare frozen linear probe, fine-tuned PCLR, and a de novo CNN matching paper-c. Metrics: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration for EF≤35; hazard ratio for incident EF≤35 among baseline EF>35 by screen status. Validate temporally and externally; benchmark against paper-c’s AUC 0.93. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no source shows PCLR embeddings encode LVEF; the continuous-probe gate is a proposed hypothesis.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We test whether PCLR self-supervised ECG representations linearly predict echocardiographic LVEF before fine-tuning for EF≤35 with limited labels. Success would establish label-efficient ALVD screening and show contrastive ECG features capture structural cardiac function.

FINAL IDEA: PCLR’s self-supervised ECG embeddings must first linearly predict continuous LVEF to justify fine-tuning on limited ECG-echo labels for screening asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction.

papers.text:
Title: Patient Contrastive Learning: a Performant, Expressive, and Practical Approach to ECG Modeling.
Abstract: Supervised machine learning applications in health care are often limited due to a scarcity of labeled training data. To mitigate this effect small sample size, we introduce pre-training approach, Patient Contrastive Learning Representations (PCLR), which creates latent representations ECGs from large number unlabeled examples. The resulting expressive, performant, and practical across wide spectrum clinical tasks. We develop PCLR using system with over 3.2 million 12-lead ECGs, demonstrate substantial improvements multiple new tasks when there fewer than 5,000 labels.

Title: Screening for cardiac contractile dysfunction using an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram
Abstract: Asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD) is present in 3-6% of the general population, is associated with reduced quality of life and longevity, and is treatable when found1-4. An inexpensive, noninvasive screening tool for ALVD in the doctor's office is not available. We tested the hypothesis that application of artificial intelligence (AI) to the electrocardiogram (ECG), a routine method of measuring the heart's electrical activity, could identify ALVD. Using paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data, including the left ventricular ejection fraction (a measure of contractile function), from 44,959 patients at the Mayo Clinic, we trained a convolutional neural network to identify patients with ventricular dysfunction, defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, using the ECG data alone. When tested on an independent set of 52,870 patients, the network model yielded values for the area under the curve, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.93, 86.3%, 85.7%, and 85.7%, respectively. In patients without ventricular dysfunction, those with a positive AI screen were at 4 times the risk (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 3.3 to 5.0) of developing future ventricular dysfunction compared with those with a negative screen. Application of AI to the ECG-a ubiquitous, low-cost test-permits the ECG to serve as a powerful screening tool in asymptomatic individuals to identify ALVD.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b: PCLR contrastive pretraining on 3.2 million unlabeled 12-lead ECGs produces expressive latent representations and improves downstream clinical tasks when fewer than 5,000 labels are available.  
Paper-c: A supervised CNN trained on 44,959 paired ECG-echocardiogram records identifies left ventricular ejection fraction ≤35%, with AUC 0.93 and sensitivity/specificity/accuracy of 86.3/85.7/85.7% on 52,870 independent records; a positive AI screen confers a 4.1-fold hazard for future ventricular dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
PCLR supplies an unsupervised ECG feature extractor; paper-c supplies a clinically validated ejection-fraction label and outcome. Operationally, PCLR’s pretrained encoder is frozen or fine-tuned for ALVD classification, replacing training from scratch and reducing dependence on expensive echo-labeled pairs. The causal connection is representational transfer: PCLR encodes general ECG morphology/rhythm features, while the ALVD head learns only to map those features to contractile dysfunction. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no known dataset overlap or identical lead preprocessing between PCLR and Mayo cohorts; it is unknown whether PCLR features retain subtle contractile-dysfunction signatures.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Use Mayo paired ECG-echo data as labeled data. Train ALVD classifiers with three encoders: PCLR-frozen, PCLR-fine-tuned, and from-scratch CNN, at label sizes of 500, 1,000, and 5,000. Validate on held-out records using AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy. For patients with normal baseline ejection fraction, compare future ventricular-dysfunction hazard ratios between positive and negative screens. Include external validation if available.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We propose combining contrastive ECG pretraining with echocardiogram-derived contractile dysfunction labels to create a low-label ALVD screening model. PCLR representations will be transferred to a Mayo ECG-echo cohort, and performance will be benchmarked against a fully supervised CNN. The study tests whether self-supervised ECG features reduce labeled-data requirements while preserving high screening accuracy and prognostic value.

FINAL IDEA: Use PCLR’s contrastive ECG representations as a pretraining stage to improve echocardiogram-labeled screening for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction, especially under scarce labeled data.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b: PCLR contrastive pretraining on >3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs creates transferable representations and improves downstream tasks with <5,000 labels.  
Paper-c: Mayo CNN on paired ECG-echo detects EF≤35% (AUC 0.93); positive screen in normal-EF patients has HR 4.1 for future dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Adopt B’s unsupervised ECG encoder and C’s validated echo-derived label. Reject C’s fully supervised architecture as the starting point; qualify C’s prognostic claim as an association, not a causal mechanism. Operationally, freeze or lightly fine-tune PCLR, then train a simple prediction head on echo-labeled ECGs. Contrastive features supply electrical morphology/rhythm structure; echo labels align that space to contractile function, reducing paired-label dependence. Missing cross-paper knowledge: exact overlap between PCLR pretraining data and Mayo cohort; whether PCLR latent space retains subtle contractile-dysfunction signatures.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Reimplement or obtain PCLR weights; pretrain on independent unlabeled 12-lead ECGs if needed. From C’s Mayo paired ECG-echo cohort, create label-scarce subsets (250, 1,000, 5,000). Train three arms: frozen PCLR + linear head, fine-tuned PCLR + head, and from-scratch CNN. Evaluate on a held-out set using AUC, sensitivity/specificity at Youden threshold, and calibration. Longitudinal secondary endpoint: among baseline EF>35% patients, compare incident EF≤35% hazard for PCLR-positive versus negative screens, adjusting for age/sex. Missing: no guaranteed external site or original PCLR weights.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We propose combining contrastive ECG pretraining with echo-labeled low-ejection-fraction detection to reduce supervised label requirements. PCLR frozen or fine-tuned models are benchmarked against from-scratch CNNs at 250–5,000 labels on Mayo ECG-echo data, with incident EF≤35% as a secondary prognostic endpoint. The contribution is a sample-efficient, clinically grounded screen separating unsupervised electrical representation from supervised contractile mapping.

FINAL IDEA: Contrastive ECG pretraining provides a sample-efficient feature backbone for echocardiogram-labeled detection of low ejection fraction and prospective risk stratification.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b: PCLR contrastive pretraining on >3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs produces transferable representations and improves downstream tasks with <5,000 labels.  
Paper-c: Supervised CNN on 44,959 paired ECG-echo records detects EF≤35% with AUC 0.93; positive screen in baseline EF>35% patients has HR 4.1 for future ventricular dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Adopt B’s use of PCLR as frozen/fine-tuned encoder and C’s clinically validated EF≤35% label. Reject assumption that PCLR already encodes contractile dysfunction; qualify C’s HR as cohort-specific association requiring re-estimation. Operationally, echo labels supervise only a lightweight head or fine-tuned last layers mapping PCLR’s cardiac-electrical features to ejection fraction, lowering paired-label demand. Missing cross-paper knowledge: PCLR-Mayo cohort overlap, lead preprocessing, and availability of original PCLR weights.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Using C’s Mayo ECG-echo data, create a temporal split. Sample label-scarce training subsets of 250, 1,000, and 5,000 patients. Compare three arms: frozen PCLR + linear head, fine-tuned PCLR, and from-scratch CNN. Validate on held-out records with AUC, sensitivity at specificity ≥85%, calibration, and accuracy. Longitudinal endpoint: among baseline EF>35% patients, compare future EF≤35% hazard for PCLR-positive vs negative screens, adjusted for age/sex, with 95% CI. Use multiple seeds to assess stability. Missing: external validation without new data.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We test whether contrastive ECG pretraining reduces echo-labeled data needs for detecting asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction and preserves prognostic value. PCLR frozen and fine-tuned models are benchmarked against from-scratch CNNs at label sizes 250–5,000 and evaluated for future EF≤35% risk. The contribution is a sample-efficient, clinically grounded screen linking self-supervised cardiac-electrical representations to contractile dysfunction, with explicit re-estimation rather than assumption of transferred performance.

FINAL IDEA: Contrastive ECG pretraining combined with echocardiogram-defined ejection fraction labels yields a data-efficient screen for low ejection fraction and future contractile decline, with all transferred performance re-validated.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- PCLR: a contrastive pre-training method that learns ECG representations from >3.2 million unlabeled 12-lead ECGs and improves clinical tasks when fewer than 5,000 labels are available.
- Mayo AI-ECG: a supervised CNN trained on paired ECG-echocardiogram data detects asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD; EF ≤35%) with AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, and identifies patients without baseline dysfunction at 4.1 times higher risk of future dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
PCLR supplies transferable ECG representations that reduce dependence on scarce labeled echocardiograms. The ALVD task supplies a clinically meaningful, validated outcome. Fine-tuning PCLR on a small labeled ECG-echo subset operatively connects self-supervised representation learning to low-label detection of contractile dysfunction and future ALVD risk.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Use PCLR pre-trained on large unlabeled 12-lead ECGs. From the Mayo-labeled ECG-echo cohort underlying the ALVD paper, create a low-label training subset of ≤5,000 ECGs. Fine-tune PCLR to predict EF ≤35% and compare against a de novo CNN and the published 0.93 AUC. Metrics: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, calibration. Secondary endpoint: among patients with baseline EF >35%, compare risk of future EF ≤35% for positive versus negative PCLR screens using hazard ratios. Validate on an independent held-out set. Missing cross-paper knowledge: exact overlap between PCLR pre-training data and the Mayo echo cohort; whether PCLR representations encode subtle contractile dysfunction before supervised fine-tuning; external-site generalizability.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
This project tests whether contrastive ECG pre-training improves screening for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction when labeled echocardiogram data are scarce. PCLR will be fine-tuned on ≤5,000 paired ECG-echo records to detect EF ≤35%, with comparison against de novo CNN training and published performance. We also evaluate whether PCLR-based positive screens predict future ventricular dysfunction. The contribution is a sample-efficient, clinically validated ECG screen combining unlabeled representation learning with contractile dysfunction detection, moving beyond either paper alone.

FINAL IDEA: Fine-tuning PCLR’s contrastive ECG representations on a small labeled ECG-echo subset provides a sample-efficient screening tool for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction and future contractile decline.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b: PCLR contrastively pre-trains on >3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs; downstream tasks improve with <5,000 labels.  
Paper-c: Supervised CNN trained on 44,959 paired ECG-echo records detects EF≤35% (AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%); a positive screen in patients with baseline EF>35% carries hazard ratio 4.1 for future ventricular dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
PCLR supplies an ECG feature extractor; paper-c supplies the validated contractile-dysfunction label and outcome. The operative link is fine-tuning PCLR embeddings with echo labels: unlabeled contrastive pretraining provides broadly cardiac-relevant representations, while supervised fine-tuning aligns those representations with ejection fraction. This differs from simple feature reuse because paper-c’s supervised CNN required paired echo labels; PCLR may not by itself encode subtle EF changes. Missing cross-paper knowledge: overlap between PCLR pre-training cohort and Mayo data, lead preprocessing, and public PCLR weights.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Using Mayo paired ECG-echo data, create label-scarce training sets of 250, 1,000, and 5,000 patients. Train EF≤35 classifiers with three conditions: PCLR linear probe, PCLR fine-tuned, and from-scratch CNN. Validate on independent held-out Mayo records using AUC, sensitivity/specificity at the published threshold, accuracy, and calibration. For patients with baseline EF>35%, re-estimate future EF≤35 hazard ratios for positive versus negative PCLR screens; do not assume the 4.1 transfer. Revising colleagues’ proposals: I adopt A/C’s label-scarce comparisons but qualify frozen-PCLR sufficiency; I reject assuming hazard or AUC transfers without re-estimation.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We test whether contrastive ECG pre-training reduces the need for expensive echocardiogram labels in screening asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction. PCLR embeddings are fine-tuned on ≤5,000 labeled ECGs to detect EF≤35%, compared with a supervised CNN, and tested for future ventricular dysfunction. The contribution is a data-efficient, clinically validated ECG screen linking unsupervised cardiac electrical representations to contractile dysfunction.

FINAL IDEA: Fine-tuning PCLR’s contrastive ECG representations on limited echocardiogram labels provides a data-efficient screen for low ejection fraction and future contractile dysfunction, while explicitly validating transferred performance rather than assuming it.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Paper-b: PCLR contrastively pre-trains on >3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs; downstream tasks improve with <5,000 labels.  
Paper-c: Supervised CNN on 44,959 paired ECG-echo records detects EF≤35% (AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%); positive screen in baseline EF>35% carries HR 4.1 for future dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
Adopt paper-b’s contrastive ECG encoder as feature backbone and paper-c’s echo-derived EF≤35 label/outcome. Reject from-scratch CNN as default and reject frozen linear probe as likely sufficient because contractile dysfunction may require subtle fine-tuning. Qualify paper-c’s HR 4.1 as model-specific association, not transferable without re-estimation. Operationally, PCLR supplies general electrical features; supervised fine-tuning aligns them to contractile function, reducing paired echo-label dependence.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Use Mayo ECG-echo cohort as labeled data; re-train PCLR on unlabeled 12-lead ECGs if weights unavailable. Create label-scarce subsets: 100, 500, 1,000, and 5,000 patients. Train three arms: from-scratch CNN, frozen PCLR + linear head, and fine-tuned PCLR + head to predict EF≤35. Validate on independent held-out temporal split using AUC, sensitivity at specificity ≥85%, accuracy, and calibration. Longitudinal secondary endpoint: among baseline EF>35% patients, estimate future EF≤35 hazard ratio for positive vs negative fine-tuned PCLR screen, adjusted for age/sex, with 95% CI and multiple random seeds. Missing cross-paper knowledge: overlap between PCLR pre-training data and Mayo ECGs, lead preprocessing, and whether PCLR latent space retains low-EF signatures.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We test whether contrastive ECG pre-training reduces echo-labeled data needs for screening asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction. PCLR frozen and fine-tuned models are benchmarked against from-scratch CNN at 100–5,000 labels, with temporal validation and future EF≤35 risk re-estimation. The contribution is a sample-efficient, clinically grounded ECG screen that separates unsupervised electrical representation from supervised contractile mapping, without assuming transferred prognostic effect.

FINAL IDEA: Fine-tuned PCLR contrastive ECG representations, validated against echo-derived EF≤35, reduce labeled-data requirements and provide a rigorous prognostic screen for future contractile dysfunction without assuming transfer of prior hazard ratios.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b (PCLR): Contrastive self-supervised pre-training on >3.2 million unlabeled 12-lead ECGs creates general ECG representations; downstream tasks improve with fewer than 5,000 labels.
- Paper-c (Mayo AI-ECG): Supervised CNN on paired ECG-echocardiogram data from 44,959 patients detects EF≤35% from ECG alone (AUC 0.93; sensitivity 86.3%; specificity 85.7%); positive screen in normal-EF patients confers hazard ratio 4.1 for future ventricular dysfunction.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use PCLR’s unsupervised ECG representations as the backbone for the ALVD screening task, then fine-tune with a small number of echocardiogram labels. Operationally, contrastive pre-training from unlabeled ECGs supplies a cardiac-electrical feature space; supervised echo labels align that space to contractile function. This should reduce required paired ECG-echo labels and allow probing of whether latent electrical remodeling precedes overt EF decline.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Reimplement PCLR on available unlabeled 12-lead ECGs. Using Mayo paired ECG-echo data, create label-scarce training subsets (100, 250, 500, 1,000, 5,000 patients) labeled EF≤35% vs >35%. Compare PCLR-fine-tuned models against a supervised CNN trained from scratch on the same subsets. Validate on an independent set with AUC, sensitivity/specificity at a fixed specificity threshold, and calibration. Longitudinal validation: among baseline EF>35% patients, compare incident EF≤35% hazard for positive vs negative PCLR screen. Missing cross-paper knowledge: no access to PCLR code/weights, pretraining corpus overlap with Mayo data, or paired echo labels beyond paper-c.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose combining contrastive self-supervised ECG pre-training with AI-ECG detection of low ejection fraction. The hypothesis is that PCLR representations require substantially fewer echo-labeled ECGs to match Mayo’s supervised CNN and that PCLR-positive normal-EF patients show elevated risk of future contractile dysfunction.

FINAL IDEA: Contrastive self-supervised ECG representations reduce label requirements for AI-ECG detection of low ejection fraction and enable early risk stratification for future contractile dysfunction.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Adopt from paper-b: PCLR contrastive pre-training on >3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs yields general representations and improves downstream tasks with <5,000 labels. Adopt from paper-c: supervised CNN on 44,959 paired ECG-echo records detects EF≤35% with AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%; positive screen in baseline EF>35% confers hazard ratio 4.1 for future dysfunction. Reject: any assumption that PCLR features automatically encode contractile-dysfunction signatures—not shown. Qualify: paper-b’s practical benefit is label-scarce transfer, not specifically ALVD screening.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
PCLR’s frozen/fine-tuned encoder supplies general cardiac-electrical features; paper-c’s echo-defined EF≤35% label supervises a lightweight head mapping those features to contractile dysfunction. This is operational transfer, not shared keywords: contrastive pre-training lowers labeled-pair demand; echo labels provide clinically validated outcome and longitudinal risk. Missing cross-paper knowledge: overlap between PCLR pre-training corpus and Mayo ECGs, lead preprocessing, and whether subtle low-EF electrical changes survive PCLR representation.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Use Mayo paired ECG-echo data. Train three encoders: PCLR-frozen, PCLR-fine-tuned, from-scratch CNN. Create label-scarce subsets of 100, 500, 1,000, and 5,000 patients. Predict EF≤35%. Validate on held-out set with AUC, sensitivity at specificity≥85%, calibration. Longitudinal: among baseline EF>35%, compare future EF≤35% hazard for positive vs negative PCLR-fine-tuned screen, adjusted for age/sex, with 95% CI. Use multiple random seeds to assess stability. Reject single-label-size validation; qualify external validation as unavailable without new data, so use internal temporal split.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We test whether PCLR contrastive ECG representations reduce paired ECG-echo labels needed to detect asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction and preserve prognostic value. PCLR-frozen and fine-tuned models are benchmarked against a from-scratch CNN at 100–5,000 labels and evaluated longitudinally for future EF≤35% risk.

FINAL IDEA: Contrastive self-supervised ECG representation learning reduces echo-labeled data requirements for detecting asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction and stratifies future contractile decline.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS  
Adopt paper-b’s PCLR contrastive pre-training on >3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs and its claim of improved downstream tasks with <5,000 labels. Adopt paper-c’s validated echo-defined EF≤35% label and its reported hazard ratio 4.1 for future dysfunction. Reject any assumption that PCLR already encodes contractile dysfunction; paper-c’s implemented supervised CNN does not transfer without re-training. Qualify paper-b’s label-efficiency as task-general, not ALVD-specific, and paper-c’s HR as an association, not a causal effect.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM  
PCLR supplies a frozen or lightly fine-tuned ECG encoder; paper-c’s echo-derived label supervises a lightweight binary head. Operationally, contrastive pre-training provides broad cardiac electrical features, while echo labels align those features to contractile dysfunction, reducing paired-label dependence. Missing cross-paper knowledge: cohort overlap, lead preprocessing, and public PCLR weights.

RESEARCH DESIGN  
Use Mayo paired ECG-echo data from paper-c. Create stratified label-scarce subsets: 250, 500, 1,000, 5,000. Train three arms: PCLR linear probe, PCLR fine-tuned, from-scratch CNN. Evaluate on indepedent held-out records with AUC, sensitivity at specificity≥85.7%, accuracy, and calibration. Longitudinal endpoint: among baseline EF>35% test patients, re-estimate future EF≤35% hazard ratio for positive versus negative PCLR-fine-tuned screen, adjusted for age/sex; do not assume 4.1. Use repeated subsampling for confidence intervals.

WORKING ABSTRACT  
We test whether PCLR contrastive ECG representations reduce echo-labeled data needs for detecting EF≤35% and preserve prognostic value. PCLR-frozen and fine-tuned models are compared with from-scratch CNNs at 250–5,000 labels on Mayo ECG-echo data, with re-estimated longitudinal risk. Contribution: a sample-efficient, validated ALVD screen separating unsupervised ECG representation from supervised contractile mapping.

FINAL IDEA: Fine-tuning PCLR’s contrastive ECG representations on limited echocardiogram labels yields a sample-efficient screen for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction and re-estimated future risk, without assuming transfer.

Title: Patient Contrastive Learning: a Performant, Expressive, and Practical Approach to ECG Modeling.
Abstract: Supervised machine learning applications in health care are often limited due to a scarcity of labeled training data. To mitigate this effect small sample size, we introduce pre-training approach, Patient Contrastive Learning Representations (PCLR), which creates latent representations ECGs from large number unlabeled examples. The resulting expressive, performant, and practical across wide spectrum clinical tasks. We develop PCLR using system with over 3.2 million 12-lead ECGs, demonstrate substantial improvements multiple new tasks when there fewer than 5,000 labels.

Title: Screening for cardiac contractile dysfunction using an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram
Abstract: Asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD) is present in 3-6% of the general population, is associated with reduced quality of life and longevity, and is treatable when found1-4. An inexpensive, noninvasive screening tool for ALVD in the doctor's office is not available. We tested the hypothesis that application of artificial intelligence (AI) to the electrocardiogram (ECG), a routine method of measuring the heart's electrical activity, could identify ALVD. Using paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data, including the left ventricular ejection fraction (a measure of contractile function), from 44,959 patients at the Mayo Clinic, we trained a convolutional neural network to identify patients with ventricular dysfunction, defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, using the ECG data alone. When tested on an independent set of 52,870 patients, the network model yielded values for the area under the curve, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.93, 86.3%, 85.7%, and 85.7%, respectively. In patients without ventricular dysfunction, those with a positive AI screen were at 4 times the risk (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 3.3 to 5.0) of developing future ventricular dysfunction compared with those with a negative screen. Application of AI to the ECG-a ubiquitous, low-cost test-permits the ECG to serve as a powerful screening tool in asymptomatic individuals to identify ALVD.

Paper-b: PCLR contributes a contrastive pre-training method for 12-lead ECG, learning expressive latent representations from >3.2 million unlabeled ECGs; it improves downstream clinical task performance when labeled data are scarce (<5,000 labels).
Second paper: Not supplied; no source contribution can be stated without inventing results or methods.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
No genuine causal or operational integration can be specified with only one paper. A valid connection would require the missing paper’s concrete method, concept, theory, or data contribution—e.g., a physiological model, wearable sensor pipeline, causal inference framework, or clinical outcome measure—to interact with PCLR’s learned ECG representations. Shared keywords or guessed disciplines are not an integration mechanism. This missing cross-paper knowledge is explicitly flagged.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
A testable cross-disciplinary design cannot be responsibly proposed. Any design would require knowing the second paper’s contribution to define measurements, validation, and the operational link to PCLR embeddings. Without that, proposing a study would invent source material.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
Unable to produce a genuine integrated abstract. Only PCLR is available; the second source paper is required to define an interdisciplinary mechanism and testable design.

FINAL IDEA: A genuine integrated research idea cannot be formed from the single available paper; the second source paper must be supplied to define a cross-disciplinary mechanism and testable design.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-b: PCLR contrastive pretraining on >3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs yields transferable patient-level embeddings; downstream tasks improve with <5,000 labels.
Paper-c (adopted from Researcher B’s delivered claims, qualified as colleague-reported, not directly verified): CNN on paired ECG-echo (n=44,959) detects left ventricular dysfunction EF≤35%, AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, accuracy 85.7%; positive screen predicts future dysfunction HR 4.1.
Rejected: Researcher C’s no-proposal stance; a provisional integration is possible using colleague-delivered paper-c constraints.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use PCLR’s pretrained ECG encoder as the backbone for paper-c’s LV-dysfunction screening. Freeze PCLR embeddings and train a lightweight head to predict EF≤35%; contrastive pretraining supplies patient-level invariance that should lower labeled-pair requirements, operationally connecting representation learning to clinical screening.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Data: Paper-b unlabeled ECGs for pretraining; paper-c paired ECG-echo cohort for fine-tuning/validation. Split paired data into 1%, 5%, 10% label subsets; hold out external site.
Model: PCLR encoder → logistic/proportional hazards head. Compare with paper-c CNN trained on same subsets and full supervision.
Measurements: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration slope; incident EF≤35% hazard ratio in baseline-normal subset; prospective echo confirmation rate.
Validation: External 12-lead ECG-echo pairs not used in pretraining; test calibration and subgroup performance by sex, age, lead availability.
Contribution: Shows whether self-supervised ECG representation reduces dependence on paired echo labels for contractile dysfunction screening, enabling low-resource deployment beyond either paper.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We propose coupling patient contrastive learning (PCLR) with AI-ECG screening for left ventricular dysfunction. PCLR pretrains on 3.2M unlabeled ECGs; its frozen embeddings train a lightweight EF≤35% classifier using only 1–10% of paired ECG-echo data. We test whether contrastive embeddings achieve comparable AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and incident dysfunction hazard ratio to a fully supervised CNN while requiring far fewer echo labels, with external validation.

FINAL IDEA: Self-supervised PCLR embeddings can make AI-ECG detection of left ventricular dysfunction data-efficient by fine-tuning a lightweight head on few paired ECG-echo labels, reducing echo dependency while preserving validated screening performance.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Adopt paper-b via colleague: PCLR contrastively pretrains on >3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs and improves downstream tasks with <5,000 labels.
Adopt paper-c via Researcher B: CNN trained on 44,959 paired ECG-echo detects EF≤35%, AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%; positive screen predicts future dysfunction HR 4.1.
Qualify: both are secondhand claims; exact PCLR architecture, lead preprocessing, and label overlap remain unverified.
Reject: Researcher C’s early no-proposal stance and any use of shared keywords as integration.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use PCLR’s frozen self-supervised ECG embeddings as input to a lightweight linear probe trained on paper-c’s echo-derived EF≤35 labels. This operatively replaces paper-c’s raw ECG feature extractor: PCLR supplies patient-level cardiac representations that encode rhythm/morphology, while the probe learns a smooth mapping to contractile dysfunction. Because embeddings are frozen, labeled paired data demand is reduced; fine-tuning entire PCLR would confound label-efficiency claims and is rejected.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Cohort: paper-c’s paired ECG-echo set; retain only ECG-echo within 30 days. Extract frozen PCLR embeddings for all ECGs. Create label-scarce training subsets: 250, 500, 1,000, 5,000 patients; 5 random seeds each. Train L2-regularized logistic regression/MLP probe on embeddings. Comparators: paper-c CNN trained from scratch on same subsets and full data; linear probe on raw 12-lead features.
Primary: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy for EF≤35 on held-out Mayo patients and external ECG-echo cohort if available.
Secondary: among baseline EF>35%, hazard ratio for incident EF≤35 using probe threshold, compared with paper-c’s HR 4.1.
Validation: calibration slope, subgroup by age/sex/lead availability, bootstrapped CIs.
Contribution: shows self-supervised ECG embeddings make echo-labeled LV dysfunction screening label-efficient and externally generalizable beyond either paper.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We test whether frozen PCLR embeddings from 3.2M unlabeled ECGs can drive paper-c’s AI-ECG screening for EF≤35% using as few as 250 labeled ECG-echo pairs. A linear probe on PCLR is compared with paper-c’s fully supervised CNN for detection and future dysfunction hazard, under external validation.

FINAL IDEA: Frozen PCLR self-supervised ECG embeddings, combined with a linear probe on paper-c’s echo-derived EF≤35 labels, can achieve label-efficient and externally valid AI screening for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-c contributes a convolutional neural network trained on paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data from 44,959 patients to identify left ventricular dysfunction (ejection fraction ≤35%) from ECG alone. It reports AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, and accuracy 85.7% on 52,870 patients. In patients without baseline dysfunction, a positive AI screen predicted future ventricular dysfunction with hazard ratio 4.1. The contribution is a validated AI-enabled screening method converting a routine, low-cost ECG into a contractile dysfunction risk signal.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Cannot be specified from available material. Only one source paper is provided; no second paper’s method, theory, data, or variables are available. Any proposed causal or operational connection would require inventing claims from the missing source. Missing cross-paper knowledge: the second paper’s domain, mechanism, and interface with AI-ECG screening.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
A valid two-source design cannot be constructed without the second paper. To avoid fabrication, no measurements, sample, or validation are proposed. If the second source is later supplied, the design should test whether paper-c’s AI-ECG screen operates causally or operationally with the second paper’s contribution—e.g., whether combining the screen with a second-source intervention changes detection rates, downstream echocardiography, or incident heart failure—using explicit variables from both papers.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
A genuine interdisciplinary proposal cannot be abstracted because only one source paper is available. A valid abstract would combine paper-c’s AI-ECG screening for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction with a second source through an explicitly stated cross-disciplinary mechanism; that mechanism is currently absent and cannot be fabricated.

FINAL IDEA: A non-fabricated two-source integration cannot be proposed from the single available paper; the missing second source must be supplied to specify a valid cross-disciplinary mechanism and testable design.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-c: A convolutional neural network trained on 44,959 paired 12-lead ECG/echocardiograms to detect left ventricular dysfunction (ejection fraction ≤35%) from ECG alone; test AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, accuracy 85.7%; among baseline-normal patients, a positive AI screen had hazard ratio 4.1 for future dysfunction.
Paper-b: Adopted from Researcher A only—PCLR, a contrastive pre-training method for 12-lead ECG, learns latent representations from >3.2 million unlabeled ECGs and improves downstream task performance under label scarcity (<5,000 labels). This is qualified as a colleague-delivered claim; the original paper-b abstract is not available to me.

Adopted: PCLR’s label-efficiency claim as a plausible bridge to paper-c.  
Rejected: Researcher A’s refusal to integrate—using the PCLR claim enables a concrete mechanism.  
Rejected: Researcher C’s statement that no source paper is available; paper-c is present.  
Qualified: Paper-b details remain unverified from the source; I use them only as a testable hypothesis.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
PCLR’s self-supervised ECG encoder provides a transferable electrophysiological feature space; paper-c contributes a clinically validated mapping from ECG features to contractile dysfunction. Operationally, the ALVD classifier is initialized with PCLR weights instead of random weights, then fine-tuned on a small labeled subset of paper-c’s paired ECG-echo data. This reduces dependence on large echocardiogram-labeled training sets and may improve generalization. Missing cross-paper knowledge: PCLR’s exact architecture, input format, and compatibility with paper-c’s 12-lead ECG pipeline.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Using paper-c’s Mayo dataset, create label-scarce subsets of N=500, 1,000, 5,000 paired ECG-echo records. Compare three models: (1) paper-c’s CNN trained from scratch on full data; (2) PCLR-pretrained encoder with a linear head, fine-tuned on each subset; (3) same PCLR encoder with low-rank adaptation. Validate on held-out Mayo patients and an external ECG-echo cohort. Primary metrics: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy for ejection fraction ≤35%. Secondary metric: hazard ratio for future ventricular dysfunction among baseline EF>35% patients using paper-c’s definition. Measurements: 12-lead ECG, echocardiographic EF, and PCLR embeddings extracted before fine-tuning.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We test whether contrastive pre-training on unlabeled 12-lead ECGs improves AI screening for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction when only small labeled ECG-echo datasets are available. We initialize paper-c’s ALVD classifier with PCLR representations, fine-tune on scarce labeled subsets, and evaluate detection accuracy and future dysfunction risk. This would combine PCLR’s label-efficient representations with paper-c’s clinically validated screening outcome, yielding a transferable low-resource ECG screening tool.

FINAL IDEA: PCLR’s self-supervised 12-lead ECG representations may enable label-efficient fine-tuning of paper-c’s AI-ECG screen for asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction, improving generalization and reducing dependency on large echocardiogram-labeled datasets.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
Paper-c (direct): CNN trained on 44,959 paired ECG-echo records detects ejection fraction ≤35% from 12-lead ECG; test AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, accuracy 85.7%; baseline-normal patients with positive screen had hazard ratio 4.1 for future dysfunction.
Paper-b via colleagues, qualified: PCLR contrastive pretraining on >3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs yields transferable embeddings; downstream tasks improve with <5,000 labels.
Adopt: PCLR label-efficiency as testable hypothesis; paper-c’s outcome definitions and validation metrics.
Reject: Researcher C’s earlier no-proposal stance; any claim that PCLR embeddings already encode cardiac structure without validation.
Qualify: PCLR architecture, embedding dimension, preprocessing, and whether paper-c patients were excluded from pretraining remain unverified.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Freeze PCLR encoder; compute patient-level embeddings for paper-c’s ECGs. Train a lightweight head (logistic regression or attention pooling) on those embeddings to predict EF≤35. This replaces paper-c’s end-to-end CNN with transferable features, operationally connecting self-supervised representation learning to clinically labeled screening. Missing cross-paper knowledge: PCLR model weights/API, input lead format, and patient overlap with Mayo data.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Use paper-c’s Mayo training/test split. Randomly subsample paired labels to n=500, 1,000, 5,000. Compare three arms: (1) frozen PCLR embeddings + linear head, (2) PCLR embeddings + low-rank adaptation, (3) paper-c CNN trained from scratch on same subsets and on full data. Validate on paper-c’s independent test set; external cohort only if obtained. Primary metrics: AUC, sensitivity/specificity at paper-c’s threshold, calibration slope/intercept. Secondary: among baseline EF>35, hazard ratio for future EF≤35 using positive screen. Report bootstrap CIs and subgroup analyses by sex/age.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We test whether frozen PCLR embeddings from self-supervised 12-lead ECGs can match paper-c’s AI screening for EF≤35 using only 1–10% of paired ECG-echo labels. A lightweight head is trained on PCLR features and validated on paper-c’s independent cohort for AUC, threshold sensitivity/specificity, calibration, and incident dysfunction hazard ratio. This would show label-efficient transferable ECG representations reduce reliance on echo-paired labels while preserving screening performance.

FINAL IDEA: Self-supervised PCLR embeddings can make paper-c’s AI-ECG left ventricular dysfunction screening label-efficient by training a lightweight head on scarce paired ECG-echo data, reducing echocardiogram dependency while preserving validated screening accuracy.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Adopt from Paper-b via colleague: PCLR contrastive pre-training on >3.2 million unlabeled 12-lead ECGs, enabling strong downstream performance with <5,000 labels.  
Adopt from Paper-c via colleague: validated CNN that screens for left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF≤35%) from ECG paired with echocardiography, reporting AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, and incident dysfunction HR 4.1.  
Reject: any invented source details beyond these secondhand claims.  
Qualify: exact PCLR architecture, ECG acquisition parameters, and label overlap are not directly verified.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Use PCLR’s frozen self-supervised ECG embeddings as input features to a lightweight head trained with Paper-c’s paired ECG-echocardiogram labels. PCLR captures cardiac structure/rhythm latently; the echo-derived LVEF≤35 label is a smooth function on those embeddings. This causally/operationally replaces raw ECG preprocessing in Paper-c and reduces labeled paired data needed for screening.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Retrospective cohort with 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram EF within 30 days. Extract frozen PCLR embeddings for all ECGs. Train logistic/MLP head on 1%, 5%, and 10% random labeled subsets for LVEF≤35. Validate against Paper-c’s fully supervised CNN: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration. In patients with baseline EF>35%, compute incident dysfunction/failure hazard ratio using output threshold. External site validation if available; report confidence intervals, subgroup by age/sex.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
We propose pairing PCLR’s contrastive ECG representations with Paper-c’s echo-labeled LV dysfunction screening task to test whether self-supervised embeddings reduce required labeled paired data while preserving screening performance and prospective risk stratification.

FINAL IDEA: Self-supervised PCLR ECG embeddings can operationalize Paper-c’s AI-ECG left ventricular dysfunction screening with substantially fewer paired echocardiogram labels, merging contrastive pre-training with echo-derived outcome prediction.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Adopt Paper-b (PCLR) from Researcher A: contrastive pre-training on >3.2M unlabeled 12-lead ECGs; label efficiency <5,000 labels. Qualify: exact encoder architecture and preprocessing not independently verified.  
Adopt Paper-c (ALVD) from Researcher B: CNN on 44,959 paired ECG-echo; AUC 0.93, sensitivity 86.3%, specificity 85.7%, accuracy 85.7%; positive screen HR 4.1 for future dysfunction. Qualify: external validation not directly available.  
Reject Researcher A’s earlier refusal to integrate; Paper-c is now supplied by Researcher B. Reject any unverified low-rank adaptation as a primary mechanism unless shown needed.  
Reject Researcher B’s low-rank adaptation arm; include only if pilot shows frozen-linear underperforms.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Freeze PCLR’s self-supervised ECG encoder and train a lightweight linear/logistic head on Paper-c’s LVEF≤35 echo labels. PCLR latently captures cardiac conduction/rhythm; the echo-derived label is a smooth function on that embedding. Missing cross-paper knowledge: PCLR input duration/lead formatting vs Paper-c’s 12-lead ECG pipeline.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Use Paper-c’s paired cohort; extract frozen PCLR embeddings. Create label-scarce random subsets N=500, 1,000, 5,000 pairs (adopt Researcher B). Compare: (1) Paper-c CNN from scratch on full data; (2) PCLR frozen encoder + linear head trained on each subset; (3) optional low-rank adapted PCLR only if (2) underperforms. Validate held-out internal site and external ECG-echo cohort. Metrics: AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration slope; pre-specified subgroup by sex/age. In baseline EF>35%, apply threshold to PCLR-head and compute HR for incident LVEF≤35 with longitudinal echo follow-up, using bootstrapped CIs.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
We test whether PCLR’s contrastively pretrained 12-lead ECG embeddings enable label-efficient screening for left ventricular dysfunction. Freezing PCLR, we train a linear head on 500–5,000 paired ECG-echo records from Paper-c’s cohort and compare performance (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, calibration) and future dysfunction HR to Paper-c’s fully supervised CNN, with external validation.

FINAL IDEA: PCLR’s frozen self-supervised ECG embeddings can replace Paper-c’s raw ECG preprocessing for left ventricular dysfunction screening, requiring only 500–5,000 echo-labeled pairs while preserving validated detection and future risk prediction.

Title: Patient Contrastive Learning: a Performant, Expressive, and Practical Approach to ECG Modeling.
Abstract: Supervised machine learning applications in health care are often limited due to a scarcity of labeled training data. To mitigate this effect small sample size, we introduce pre-training approach, Patient Contrastive Learning Representations (PCLR), which creates latent representations ECGs from large number unlabeled examples. The resulting expressive, performant, and practical across wide spectrum clinical tasks. We develop PCLR using system with over 3.2 million 12-lead ECGs, demonstrate substantial improvements multiple new tasks when there fewer than 5,000 labels.

Title: Screening for cardiac contractile dysfunction using an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram
Abstract: Asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD) is present in 3-6% of the general population, is associated with reduced quality of life and longevity, and is treatable when found1-4. An inexpensive, noninvasive screening tool for ALVD in the doctor's office is not available. We tested the hypothesis that application of artificial intelligence (AI) to the electrocardiogram (ECG), a routine method of measuring the heart's electrical activity, could identify ALVD. Using paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data, including the left ventricular ejection fraction (a measure of contractile function), from 44,959 patients at the Mayo Clinic, we trained a convolutional neural network to identify patients with ventricular dysfunction, defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, using the ECG data alone. When tested on an independent set of 52,870 patients, the network model yielded values for the area under the curve, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.93, 86.3%, 85.7%, and 85.7%, respectively. In patients without ventricular dysfunction, those with a positive AI screen were at 4 times the risk (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 3.3 to 5.0) of developing future ventricular dysfunction compared with those with a negative screen. Application of AI to the ECG-a ubiquitous, low-cost test-permits the ECG to serve as a powerful screening tool in asymptomatic individuals to identify ALVD.

By initializing the ALVD classifier with PCLR representations and fine-tuning on small labeled ECG/echo subsets, we test whether label-efficient training matches or exceeds the original CNN while preserving prospective risk prediction. This bridges self-supervised ML methodology with cardiology screening, reducing annotation and deployment costs.

FINAL IDEA: Use PCLR’s patient-level contrastive ECG pre-training to make Paper-c’s AI-ECG ALVD screen label-efficient under scarce labeled data while preserving clinical screening accuracy and prospective risk prediction.

We propose replacing Paper-c’s randomly initialized ALVD CNN with PCLR’s self-supervised patient-level ECG encoder, fine-tuned on scarce echocardiogram labels. The study tests whether contrastive pre-training preserves screening accuracy and prospective incident-dysfunction risk at ≤1,000 labels, enabling low-resource deployment beyond either paper alone.

FINAL IDEA: PCLR’s patient-level contrastive ECG pre-training makes Paper-c’s validated ALVD screen label-efficient and transportable, tested by fine-tuning on scarce echo labels while preserving screening accuracy and incident-dysfunction hazard.

papers.text:
Title: Patient Contrastive Learning: a Performant, Expressive, and Practical Approach to ECG Modeling.
Abstract: Supervised machine learning applications in health care are often limited due to a scarcity of labeled training data. To mitigate this effect small sample size, we introduce pre-training approach, Patient Contrastive Learning Representations (PCLR), which creates latent representations ECGs from large number unlabeled examples. The resulting expressive, performant, and practical across wide spectrum clinical tasks. We develop PCLR using system with over 3.2 million 12-lead ECGs, demonstrate substantial improvements multiple new tasks when there fewer than 5,000 labels.

Title: Screening for cardiac contractile dysfunction using an artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiogram
Abstract: Asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction (ALVD) is present in 3-6% of the general population, is associated with reduced quality of life and longevity, and is treatable when found1-4. An inexpensive, noninvasive screening tool for ALVD in the doctor's office is not available. We tested the hypothesis that application of artificial intelligence (AI) to the electrocardiogram (ECG), a routine method of measuring the heart's electrical activity, could identify ALVD. Using paired 12-lead ECG and echocardiogram data, including the left ventricular ejection fraction (a measure of contractile function), from 44,959 patients at the Mayo Clinic, we trained a convolutional neural network to identify patients with ventricular dysfunction, defined as ejection fraction ≤35%, using the ECG data alone. When tested on an independent set of 52,870 patients, the network model yielded values for the area under the curve, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy of 0.93, 86.3%, 85.7%, and 85.7%, respectively. In patients without ventricular dysfunction, those with a positive AI screen were at 4 times the risk (hazard ratio, 4.1; 95% confidence interval, 3.3 to 5.0) of developing future ventricular dysfunction compared with those with a negative screen. Application of AI to the ECG-a ubiquitous, low-cost test-permits the ECG to serve as a powerful screening tool in asymptomatic individuals to identify ALVD.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- [paper-b] Qubitization block-encodes \(H=(\langle G|\otimes I)U(|G\rangle\otimes I)\), embedding \(H\) in an invariant SU(2) subspace. It gives optimal query complexity \(O(t+\log(1/\epsilon))\), at most two ancilla qubits, subsumes sparse/LCU Hamiltonians, and supports density-matrix Hamiltonians and general operator functions.
- [paper-c] Quantum signal processing (QSP) uses single-qubit rotations: transduce Hamiltonian eigenvalues into one ancilla qubit, apply an optimal-length rotation sequence, and project. It achieves \(O(td\|H\|_{\max}+\log(1/\epsilon)/\log\log(1/\epsilon))\) queries for d-sparse Hamiltonians.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Use qubitization as the eigenvalue-transduction front-end for QSP. Qubitization’s SU(2) embedding produces eigenphases \(\theta_j=\arccos(\lambda_j/\alpha)\) for Hamiltonian eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\). QSP then consumes these phases with rotation angles approximating \(f(x)=e^{-i\alpha t x}\) on \(x\in[-1,1]\), and the final projection yields \(e^{-iHt}\). This should combine qubitization’s broad input model and low ancilla overhead with QSP’s non-asymptotic \(\log\log(1/\epsilon)\) precision scaling. Missing cross-paper knowledge: neither abstract states whether QSP phase factors can be directly optimized for qubitization’s \(\arccos\)-transformed spectrum while preserving optimality and low overhead; this assumption must be tested.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Benchmark the proposed “qubitized-QSP” compiler on random density-matrix Hamiltonians \(H=\rho\) for 4–8 qubits. Encode \(\rho\) via qubitization oracles. Compute QSP phase factors for \(f(x)=e^{-i\alpha t x}\). Compare against qubitization-only and d-sparse QSP baselines. Measure query count, gate count, ancilla count, and worst-case spectral-norm error versus exact \(e^{-i\rho t}\). Fix \(t\) and vary \(\epsilon=10^{-2}\) to \(10^{-10}\); validate error scaling \(\log(1/\epsilon)/\log\log(1/\epsilon)\) at constant ancilla count. If QSP phase-factor optimization fails for the \(\arccos\) spectrum, document necessary modifications.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We combine qubitization’s oracle-based SU(2) block encoding with quantum signal processing’s optimal rotation sequences. The proposal tests whether qubitization can serve as the transduction step for QSP, yielding a unified low-ancilla simulator for non-sparse and density-matrix Hamiltonians with loglog precision scaling. Numerical benchmarks on random density matrices compare query/gate costs, ancilla overhead, and spectral error to d-sparse QSP and qubitization-only baselines.

FINAL IDEA: Use qubitization’s SU(2) block encoding as the eigenvalue-transduction front-end for quantum signal processing’s optimal rotation sequences to simulate non-sparse and density-matrix Hamiltonians with low ancilla overhead and non-asymptotic loglog precision scaling.

SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- [paper-b] Qubitization block-encodes \(H=(\langle G|\otimes I)U(|G\rangle\otimes I)\) into an invariant SU(2) subspace using controlled \(U,G\); query complexity \(O(t+\log(1/\epsilon))\), at most two ancilla qubits; supports density-matrix Hamiltonians and general operator functions.
- [paper-c] Quantum signal processing transduces eigenvalues into one ancilla qubit, applies optimal single-qubit rotation phases, and projects; gives \(O(td\|H\|_{\max}+\log(1/\epsilon)/\log\log(1/\epsilon))\) for \(d\)-sparse Hamiltonians.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Adopt: use qubitization as the eigenvalue-transduction front-end for QSP. Controlled \(U,G\) generate SU(2) eigenphases \(\theta_j=\arccos(\lambda_j/\alpha)\). Qualify: paper-c’s phase sequences were built for sparse-access spectra; applying them to arbitrary block-encoded spectra is a hypothesis, not a stated result. Reject: the claim that sparse-optimized phases automatically transfer with optimality to qubitized density matrices. Missing cross-paper knowledge: existence and stability of QSP phase factors for the \(\arccos\)-transformed qubitization spectrum.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Target density-matrix Hamiltonians \(H=\rho\) (paper-b’s motivating instance) and \(d\)-sparse baselines. Construct random block-encoded instances for 4–8 qubits. For each, build qubitized controlled-\(U/G\) circuit; compute QSP phase angles for \(f(x)=e^{-i\alpha t x}\) using Remez-type optimization. Measure: total queries to \(U,G\), ancilla count, circuit depth, spectral-norm error versus exact \(e^{-i\rho t}\). Vary \(t\) and \(\epsilon=10^{-2}\)–\(10^{-10}\). Test whether error scales as \(\log(1/\epsilon)/\log\log(1/\epsilon)\) with constant ancillas, distinct from paper-b’s asymptotic \(O(\log(1/\epsilon))\). Validate against paper-c’s sparse bound and paper-b’s low-ancilla claim. Report phase-factor convergence failures.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We combine qubitization’s general block encoding with quantum signal processing’s optimal rotation sequences, using qubitization as the transduction stage for QSP. Numerical benchmarks on random density matrices test whether explicit QSP phases for the \(\arccos\)-transformed spectrum preserve low ancilla overhead while achieving non-asymptotic loglog precision scaling. This clarifies whether qubitization’s broad input model and QSP’s phase design are operationally composable beyond sparse access.

FINAL IDEA: Use qubitization’s SU(2) block encoding as the eigenvalue-transduction stage for quantum signal processing to test whether explicit rotation phases can simulate density-matrix Hamiltonians with low ancilla overhead and loglog precision scaling.

- [paper-c] Quantum signal processing transduces eigenvalues into one ancilla qubit, applies optimal rotation phases, and projects; achieves \(O(td\|H\|_{\max}+\log(1/\epsilon)/\log\log(1/\epsilon))\) for d-sparse Hamiltonians.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:

Qualify: paper-c’s sparse-access QSP phases are not directly reusable under qubitization’s \(\arccos\)-transformed spectrum; they must be recomputed. RESEARCH DESIGN:
Test on density-matrix Hamiltonians \(H=\rho\), paper-b’s motivating instance. Construct random 4–8 qubit normalized \(\rho\) and build qubitization oracles \(U,G\) via purification. Compute QSP phase angles with Remez-type optimization for \(f(x)=e^{-i\alpha t x}\) under the arccos mapping. Measure total queries to \(U,G\), ancilla count, circuit depth, and spectral-norm error versus exact \(e^{-i\rho t}\). Sweep \(\epsilon=10^{-2}\)–\(10^{-10}\) and \(t=1,10,100\). Compare fitted phase-sequence length against \(O(t+\log(1/\epsilon))\) and \(O(t+\log(1/\epsilon)/\log\log(1/\epsilon))\). Validate success probability near unity after projection.
